skills.description: Use when a sample-by-taxon abundance/count table (e.g. flower samples x arthropod OTUs from eDNA metabarcoding) must be compared across sample groups to visualize whether communities cluster by the source species.
skills.name: community-composition-heatmap-visualization
skills.search_text: community-composition-heatmap-visualization Use when a sample-by-taxon abundance/count table (e.g. flower samples x arthropod OTUs from eDNA metabarcoding) must be compared across sample groups to visualize whether communities cluster by the source species. Input is a raw sequencing read file (FASTQ) rather than a processed OTU/count table — metabarcoding bioinformatics must be done first The analysis goal requires formal hypothesis testing of group differences (e.g. RDA, PERMANOVA) rather than a visual dendrogram/heatmap Count data should be compared with abundance-sensitive indices such as Bray-Curtis when dominant-taxa weighting is desired rather than down-weighted by cube-root transformation http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A visualization skill that turns a plant-species x arthropod-OTU count table into a Raup-Crick dissimilarity matrix, clusters samples by average linkage (UPGMA), and renders the clustered dendrogram as a pheatmap heatmap to assess whether arthropod eDNA communities segregate by plant species. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.4809
skills.summary: A visualization skill that turns a plant-species x arthropod-OTU count table into a Raup-Crick dissimilarity matrix, clusters samples by average linkage (UPGMA), and renders the clustered dendrogram as a pheatmap heatmap to assess whether arthropod eDNA communities segregate by plant species.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw sequencing read file (FASTQ) rather than a processed OTU/count table — metabarcoding bioinformatics must be done first The analysis goal requires formal hypothesis testing of group differences (e.g. RDA, PERMANOVA) rather than a visual dendrogram/heatmap Count data should be compared with abundance-sensitive indices such as Bray-Curtis when dominant-taxa weighting is desired rather than down-weighted by cube-root transformation

skills.description: Use when a DADA2-inferred, replicate-filtered MOTU table has been taxonomically assigned and you need per-species, per-family, or per-order read fractions to characterize community dominance and compare marker sets.
skills.name: community-dominance-analysis
skills.search_text: community-dominance-analysis Use when a DADA2-inferred, replicate-filtered MOTU table has been taxonomically assigned and you need per-species, per-family, or per-order read fractions to characterize community dominance and compare marker sets. Input is raw FASTQ reads that have not yet gone through DADA2 MOTU inference and replicate filtering You need presence/absence occupancy patterns or community clustering by plant species rather than quantitative read-share dominance MOTU taxonomy has not been assigned, so reads cannot be attributed to arthropod species http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Quantifies per-taxon read-share fractions in an eDNA metabarcoding dataset to identify which species dominate the community, e.g. Thrips major at 30% of COI reads and Meligethes planiusculus at 51% of 16S reads in the flower-eDNA study. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.4809
skills.summary: Quantifies per-taxon read-share fractions in an eDNA metabarcoding dataset to identify which species dominate the community, e.g. Thrips major at 30% of COI reads and Meligethes planiusculus at 51% of 16S reads in the flower-eDNA study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ reads that have not yet gone through DADA2 MOTU inference and replicate filtering You need presence/absence occupancy patterns or community clustering by plant species rather than quantitative read-share dominance MOTU taxonomy has not been assigned, so reads cannot be attributed to arthropod species

skills.description: Use when long reads (PacBio/ONT) have ambiguous probabilistic mapping scores across multiple candidate locations in a large RefSeq database and you need composition-aware resolution plus sample composition estimation.
skills.name: composition-dependent-mapping-posterior-computation
skills.search_text: composition-dependent-mapping-posterior-computation Use when long reads (PacBio/ONT) have ambiguous probabilistic mapping scores across multiple candidate locations in a large RefSeq database and you need composition-aware resolution plus sample composition estimation. Samples dominated by short reads — the minimizer-based approximate mapping underlying the posteriors requires sufficiently long reads; short reads end up with minimizer sets too small for reliable mapping locations Samples with many non-characterized (novel) entities absent from the database — no explicit genomic-divergence term is in the model, so novel strains/species cannot be explicitly detected You only need raw candidate mapping locations without composition-aware disambiguation — the approximate mapping stage (MashMap-based) alone suffices http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Recomputes each long read's candidate mapping posteriors weighted by the current genome-composition vector F (P_r(i;F) = P_r(i)·(1/E_{r;g})·F_g) inside MetaMaps' EM loop, and assigns each read to its maximum-likelihood genome once F converges. This borrows information across reads to disambiguate closely related RefSeq genomes and yields the sample composition estimate. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-10934-2
skills.summary: Recomputes each long read's candidate mapping posteriors weighted by the current genome-composition vector F (P_r(i;F) = P_r(i)·(1/E_{r;g})·F_g) inside MetaMaps' EM loop, and assigns each read to its maximum-likelihood genome once F converges. This borrows information across reads to disambiguate closely related RefSeq genomes and yields the sample composition estimate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Samples dominated by short reads — the minimizer-based approximate mapping underlying the posteriors requires sufficiently long reads; short reads end up with minimizer sets too small for reliable mapping locations Samples with many non-characterized (novel) entities absent from the database — no explicit genomic-divergence term is in the model, so novel strains/species cannot be explicitly detected You only need raw candidate mapping locations without composition-aware disambiguation — the approximate mapping stage (MashMap-based) alone suffices

skills.description: Reference for testing which taxa differ in relative abundance between sample groups when the input is a 16S rRNA ASV/OTU count table, since sequencing provides only relative abundance information.
skills.name: compositional-data-analysis
skills.search_text: compositional-data-analysis Reference for testing which taxa differ in relative abundance between sample groups when the input is a 16S rRNA ASV/OTU count table, since sequencing provides only relative abundance information. The abundance table is already transformed to relative abundance (column totals equal to 1) — ANCOM requires the absolute table The goal is a different analysis such as computing diversity metrics — the paper states whether rarefying is advisable for such analyses is beyond its scope A single tool's result will be reported without running several methods — the authors recommend a consensus approach based on multiple DA methods http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Treat 16S rRNA read counts as compositional data (CoDa) rather than absolute abundances, using log-ratio based differential abundance tools (ALDEx2, ANCOM-II) that analyze ratios of read counts between taxa, with ANCOM-II-style zero handling and prevalence filtering before testing. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-28034-z
skills.summary: Treat 16S rRNA read counts as compositional data (CoDa) rather than absolute abundances, using log-ratio based differential abundance tools (ALDEx2, ANCOM-II) that analyze ratios of read counts between taxa, with ANCOM-II-style zero handling and prevalence filtering before testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The abundance table is already transformed to relative abundance (column totals equal to 1) — ANCOM requires the absolute table The goal is a different analysis such as computing diversity metrics — the paper states whether rarefying is advisable for such analyses is beyond its scope A single tool's result will be reported without running several methods — the authors recommend a consensus approach based on multiple DA methods

skills.description: Use when a compositional abundance table (SGB/species relative abundances) must be log-transformed before per-taxon statistical testing, e.g. fitting diet-association mixed models on mouse gut MetaPhlAn 4 profiles.
skills.name: compositional-data-clr-transformation
skills.search_text: compositional-data-clr-transformation Use when a compositional abundance table (SGB/species relative abundances) must be log-transformed before per-taxon statistical testing, e.g. fitting diet-association mixed models on mouse gut MetaPhlAn 4 profiles. Input is already a log-transformed or absolute-count feature table rather than compositional relative abundances Profiling has not yet been run — raw shotgun reads must first be converted to a SGB abundance profile (e.g. with MetaPhlAn 4) before CLR can be applied http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Applies a centered log-ratio (CLR) transform to compositional taxonomic abundance tables (e.g. MetaPhlAn 4 SGB relative abundances), adding a pseudocount to zeros before the log transform so that abundance data become suitable for downstream differential-abundance modeling such as linear mixed models. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41587-023-01688-w
skills.summary: Applies a centered log-ratio (CLR) transform to compositional taxonomic abundance tables (e.g. MetaPhlAn 4 SGB relative abundances), adding a pseudocount to zeros before the log transform so that abundance data become suitable for downstream differential-abundance modeling such as linear mixed models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a log-transformed or absolute-count feature table rather than compositional relative abundances Profiling has not yet been run — raw shotgun reads must first be converted to a SGB abundance profile (e.g. with MetaPhlAn 4) before CLR can be applied

skills.description: Use when an observed OTU/feature count table (taxa x samples) plus metadata with a discrete grouping variable must be tested for taxa whose absolute abundance differs between groups, while correcting for unequal sampling fractions across samples.
skills.name: compositional-data-differential-abundance-analysis
skills.search_text: compositional-data-differential-abundance-analysis Use when an observed OTU/feature count table (taxa x samples) plus metadata with a discrete grouping variable must be tested for taxa whose absolute abundance differs between groups, while correcting for unequal sampling fractions across samples. Sample sizes are very small (e.g. n = 5 per group): the article states ANCOM-BC may not perform well and FDR is not controlled in such cases The proportion of differentially abundant taxa is too large: FDR may be slightly elevated The grouping variable is continuous or the goal is correlation estimation rather than discrete-group DA: ANCOM-BC v1.0 only supports discrete group.var http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Performs differential abundance (DA) analysis of microbiome count data with ANCOM-BC, which recasts DA as a log-scale linear regression with a sample-specific offset that estimates and corrects the sampling-fraction bias, yielding p-values, confidence intervals, and FDR control that compositionality-blind or ANCOM-style methods lack. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17041-7
skills.summary: Performs differential abundance (DA) analysis of microbiome count data with ANCOM-BC, which recasts DA as a log-scale linear regression with a sample-specific offset that estimates and corrects the sampling-fraction bias, yielding p-values, confidence intervals, and FDR control that compositionality-blind or ANCOM-style methods lack.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sample sizes are very small (e.g. n = 5 per group): the article states ANCOM-BC may not perform well and FDR is not controlled in such cases The proportion of differentially abundant taxa is too large: FDR may be slightly elevated The grouping variable is continuous or the goal is correlation estimation rather than discrete-group DA: ANCOM-BC v1.0 only supports discrete group.var

skills.description: Use when a raw OTU/taxon-by-sample abundance table plus metadata must be cleaned before ANCOM-BC or normalization-comparison workflows: sparse taxa, low-library-size samples, and per-group structural zeros need handling.
skills.name: compositional-data-preprocessing
skills.search_text: compositional-data-preprocessing Use when a raw OTU/taxon-by-sample abundance table plus metadata must be cleaned before ANCOM-BC or normalization-comparison workflows: sparse taxa, low-library-size samples, and per-group structural zeros need handling. group.var is continuous or ordinal — ANCOM-BC v1.0 only supports a discrete group.var The goal is DA testing for taxa that are structural zeros across all samples — ANCOM-BC/ANCOM-BC2 are not designed to detect differences for such taxa (handled by the presence/absence test in the packaged version) Sample sizes are very small (e.g. n = 5 per group) and FDR control is critical http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Preprocess an absolute-abundance feature table and metadata with ANCOM-BC's feature_table_pre_process before differential abundance analysis, filtering sparse taxa and low-library samples and classifying structural zeros per group via an asymptotic lower bound. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17041-7
skills.summary: Preprocess an absolute-abundance feature table and metadata with ANCOM-BC's feature_table_pre_process before differential abundance analysis, filtering sparse taxa and low-library samples and classifying structural zeros per group via an asymptotic lower bound.
skills.when_to_use_negative: group.var is continuous or ordinal — ANCOM-BC v1.0 only supports a discrete group.var The goal is DA testing for taxa that are structural zeros across all samples — ANCOM-BC/ANCOM-BC2 are not designed to detect differences for such taxa (handled by the presence/absence test in the packaged version) Sample sizes are very small (e.g. n = 5 per group) and FDR control is critical

skills.description: Use when you need to test whether differential abundance tool outputs scale with dataset characteristics such as effect size, sample size, sequencing depth, or sparsity, or to assess how prevalence filtering changes those relationships.
skills.name: compositional-data-sparsity-quantification
skills.search_text: compositional-data-sparsity-quantification Use when you need to test whether differential abundance tool outputs scale with dataset characteristics such as effect size, sample size, sequencing depth, or sparsity, or to assess how prevalence filtering changes those relationships. You need a direct recommendation of a single best DA tool rather than a characterization of how significance counts scale with data characteristics Your datasets have no two-group comparison, so no PERMANOVA effect size on Aitchison distance can be computed You want absolute false positive rates rather than correlations with dataset properties — use the false positive analysis scripts (run_all_FP_datasets_*.sh) instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Quantifies whether the percent of significant ASVs identified by each of 14 differential abundance tools correlates with dataset characteristics (PERMANOVA effect size on Aitchison distance, sample size, read depth, richness, sparsity), separately for 38 unfiltered and 10%-prevalence-filtered 16S rRNA gene datasets. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-28034-z
skills.summary: Quantifies whether the percent of significant ASVs identified by each of 14 differential abundance tools correlates with dataset characteristics (PERMANOVA effect size on Aitchison distance, sample size, read depth, richness, sparsity), separately for 38 unfiltered and 10%-prevalence-filtered 16S rRNA gene datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need a direct recommendation of a single best DA tool rather than a characterization of how significance counts scale with data characteristics Your datasets have no two-group comparison, so no PERMANOVA effect size on Aitchison distance can be computed You want absolute false positive rates rather than correlations with dataset properties — use the false positive analysis scripts (run_all_FP_datasets_*.sh) instead

skills.description: Use when you must reproduce or extend resource measurements (peak RAM, CPU hours, runtime slowdown factors) for a tool run in both default and memory-limited modes, e.g. verifying MetaMaps' claimed 1.2-1.4x slowdown at 28 GB / 16 GB targets.
skills.name: computational-resource-benchmarking
skills.search_text: computational-resource-benchmarking Use when you must reproduce or extend resource measurements (peak RAM, CPU hours, runtime slowdown factors) for a tool run in both default and memory-limited modes, e.g. verifying MetaMaps' claimed 1.2-1.4x slowdown at 28 GB / 16 GB targets. You only need a single production run and have enough RAM (e.g. 262 GB) for default mode — benchmarking mode trade-offs adds no value Your samples have a high proportion of short reads or complex, poorly characterized entities — MetaMaps itself is out of scope, so its resource trade-offs are not the right thing to benchmark You need wall-clock accounting of streaming/real-time analysis — MetaMaps does not support streaming data http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmark a metagenomic classifier's runtime, peak RAM, and accuracy trade-offs across its default and memory-constrained execution modes. For MetaMaps, this means quantifying how the heuristic '--maxmemory' memory-efficient mapping mode increases CPU time relative to default mode (which needs 262 GB RAM for a >12,000-genome RefSeq database) while confirming classification accuracy is preserved. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-10934-2
skills.summary: Benchmark a metagenomic classifier's runtime, peak RAM, and accuracy trade-offs across its default and memory-constrained execution modes. For MetaMaps, this means quantifying how the heuristic '--maxmemory' memory-efficient mapping mode increases CPU time relative to default mode (which needs 262 GB RAM for a >12,000-genome RefSeq database) while confirming classification accuracy is preserved.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need a single production run and have enough RAM (e.g. 262 GB) for default mode — benchmarking mode trade-offs adds no value Your samples have a high proportion of short reads or complex, poorly characterized entities — MetaMaps itself is out of scope, so its resource trade-offs are not the right thing to benchmark You need wall-clock accounting of streaming/real-time analysis — MetaMaps does not support streaming data

skills.description: Use when an eDNA-derived species list (e.g. resolved arthropod taxa from flower metabarcoding at a known site) needs validation against independent occurrence records, and reported concordance percentages must be reproduced or verified.
skills.name: concordance-statistic-reproduction
skills.search_text: concordance-statistic-reproduction Use when an eDNA-derived species list (e.g. resolved arthropod taxa from flower metabarcoding at a known site) needs validation against independent occurrence records, and reported concordance percentages must be reproduced or verified. The input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) or reads rather than a curated, taxonomically resolved species list — the skill presupposes taxa already resolved from the metabarcoding pipeline. The taxa of interest are from a locality outside the coverage of Naturbasen/allearter and Fauna Europaea, so absence of records cannot be distinguished from database-coverage gaps. The goal is community-structure analysis (e.g. clustering of arthropod communities by plant species), not validation of detection concordance against occurrence records. http://edamontology.org/topic_3050 Cross-references a resolved eDNA metabarcoding species list against independent public faunistic occurrence databases (Naturbasen/allearter and Fauna Europaea) and reproduces reported concordance counts/percentages at nested geographic scales (locality and island), providing an independent sanity check on metabarcoding detections. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.4809
skills.summary: Cross-references a resolved eDNA metabarcoding species list against independent public faunistic occurrence databases (Naturbasen/allearter and Fauna Europaea) and reproduces reported concordance counts/percentages at nested geographic scales (locality and island), providing an independent sanity check on metabarcoding detections.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) or reads rather than a curated, taxonomically resolved species list — the skill presupposes taxa already resolved from the metabarcoding pipeline. The taxa of interest are from a locality outside the coverage of Naturbasen/allearter and Fauna Europaea, so absence of records cannot be distinguished from database-coverage gaps. The goal is community-structure analysis (e.g. clustering of arthropod communities by plant species), not validation of detection concordance against occurrence records.

skills.description: Use when you have per-habitat bespoke taxonomic weights (from q2-clawback generate_class_weights) and per-habitat species-level classification error rates, and need to test whether habitat-specific sequence confusability explains those error rates.
skills.name: confusion-index-estimation-from-weights
skills.search_text: confusion-index-estimation-from-weights Use when you have per-habitat bespoke taxonomic weights (from q2-clawback generate_class_weights) and per-habitat species-level classification error rates, and need to test whether habitat-specific sequence confusability explains those error rates. The sample's habitat lacks sufficient characterization for bespoke weight assembly — for such natural sample types the article recommends average weights estimated from global microbial species distributions instead, so there is no weighted reference distribution to sample pairs from. You need to improve classification directly rather than explain its error structure — this skill is a diagnostic of error rates, not a classifier; use q2-feature-classifier with the habitat's bespoke weights for classification itself. Only a single habitat is available — the skill requires joining per-habitat confusion indices with per-habitat error rates across multiple environments to fit the correlation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Estimates a per-habitat confusion index — the log of the expected taxonomic distance between Greengenes-labeled species pairs that are k-mer-similar — by sampling sequence pairs from bespoke (clawback-derived) taxonomic weights, then tests how well it predicts per-habitat species-level classification error rates. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12669-6
skills.summary: Estimates a per-habitat confusion index — the log of the expected taxonomic distance between Greengenes-labeled species pairs that are k-mer-similar — by sampling sequence pairs from bespoke (clawback-derived) taxonomic weights, then tests how well it predicts per-habitat species-level classification error rates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample's habitat lacks sufficient characterization for bespoke weight assembly — for such natural sample types the article recommends average weights estimated from global microbial species distributions instead, so there is no weighted reference distribution to sample pairs from. You need to improve classification directly rather than explain its error structure — this skill is a diagnostic of error rates, not a classifier; use q2-feature-classifier with the habitat's bespoke weights for classification itself. Only a single habitat is available — the skill requires joining per-habitat confusion indices with per-habitat error rates across multiple environments to fit the correlation.

skills.description: Use when classifying EMP samples into EMPO level 2/3 environment categories from Deblur community composition and you must report cross-validated confusion matrices with overall accuracy (target ~91% and ~84%).
skills.name: confusion-matrix-accuracy-computation
skills.search_text: confusion-matrix-accuracy-computation Use when classifying EMP samples into EMPO level 2/3 environment categories from Deblur community composition and you must report cross-validated confusion matrices with overall accuracy (target ~91% and ~84%). Input is raw amplicon reads rather than a Deblur-processed BIOM feature table — the sequences must first be processed with Deblur into exact-sequence features. Samples lack EMPO level 2/3 environment annotations, so no reliable class labels exist for supervised training or a meaningful confusion matrix. The goal is feature/taxon-specific sample search rather than supervised classification — redbiom metadata and feature searches are the appropriate tool instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Builds out-of-fold confusion matrices and overall accuracy metrics for supervised classification of EMP 16S samples into EMPO environment categories, serving as the validation step for random-forest provenance classification. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/nature24621
skills.summary: Builds out-of-fold confusion matrices and overall accuracy metrics for supervised classification of EMP 16S samples into EMPO environment categories, serving as the validation step for random-forest provenance classification.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw amplicon reads rather than a Deblur-processed BIOM feature table — the sequences must first be processed with Deblur into exact-sequence features. Samples lack EMPO level 2/3 environment annotations, so no reliable class labels exist for supervised training or a meaningful confusion matrix. The goal is feature/taxon-specific sample search rather than supervised classification — redbiom metadata and feature searches are the appropriate tool instead.

skills.description: Use when you have significant-ASV result tables from multiple DA tools (14 tools in the Nearing et al. 2022 pipeline) run over many datasets (38 filtered + 38 unfiltered) and need to measure how much the tools' significant-feature sets overlap and whether prevalence filtering increases agreement.
skills.name: consensus-asv-tally-across-datasets
skills.search_text: consensus-asv-tally-across-datasets Use when you have significant-ASV result tables from multiple DA tools (14 tools in the Nearing et al. 2022 pipeline) run over many datasets (38 filtered + 38 unfiltered) and need to measure how much the tools' significant-feature sets overlap and whether prevalence filtering increases agreement. You only ran a single DA tool on a single dataset — there are no tool pairs to compute Jaccard overlap or consensus tallies across You need absolute truth about which ASVs are truly differential — this skill measures inter-tool agreement only; the paper warns the intersection of tool outputs may be the same noise The ASV table has not been preprocessed with the same prevalence filter (-F 0.1) across the compared runs — filtered/unfiltered consensus proportions are not comparable http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantify cross-tool consensus by tallying, per ASV, how many of the 14 differential abundance tools called it significantly DA, then compare consensus structure between 10% prevalence-filtered and unfiltered 16S rRNA runs (filtered data showed 38.6% vs 17.3% mean of ASVs called by >12 tools). Supports the paper's recommendation to focus on features identified by most tools. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-28034-z
skills.summary: Quantify cross-tool consensus by tallying, per ASV, how many of the 14 differential abundance tools called it significantly DA, then compare consensus structure between 10% prevalence-filtered and unfiltered 16S rRNA runs (filtered data showed 38.6% vs 17.3% mean of ASVs called by >12 tools). Supports the paper's recommendation to focus on features identified by most tools.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only ran a single DA tool on a single dataset — there are no tool pairs to compute Jaccard overlap or consensus tallies across You need absolute truth about which ASVs are truly differential — this skill measures inter-tool agreement only; the paper warns the intersection of tool outputs may be the same noise The ASV table has not been preprocessed with the same prevalence filter (-F 0.1) across the compared runs — filtered/unfiltered consensus proportions are not comparable

skills.description: Use when an OTU/ASV community matrix has a categorical metadata variable (e.g. plant species) and numeric covariates (e.g. latitude/longitude), and the goal is to visualize and permutation-test whether communities cluster by that category.
skills.name: constrained-ordination-analysis
skills.search_text: constrained-ordination-analysis Use when an OTU/ASV community matrix has a categorical metadata variable (e.g. plant species) and numeric covariates (e.g. latitude/longitude), and the goal is to visualize and permutation-test whether communities cluster by that category. The community matrix is not sample-by-taxon (e.g. only a taxon list or abundance summary without matching metadata) — ordination requires the full matrix plus per-sample species/covariate annotations. The analysis question is unconstrained pattern description of community structure without a categorical hypothesis variable — an unconstrained ordination (PCA/PCoA/NMDS) is then more appropriate than RDA with Condition(). Metadata lack geographic covariates or there is no covariate to condition on, making a partial RDA (Condition(latitude, longitude)) mismatched to the design. http://edamontology.org/topic_3050 Applies partial redundancy analysis (RDA) in vegan to eDNA metabarcoding community matrices (e.g. flower-surface arthropod OTU/ASV tables from COI/16S amplicons) to test whether biological communities are constrained by a categorical factor such as plant species, after removing geographic covariates (latitude/longitude) via Condition(). metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.4809
skills.summary: Applies partial redundancy analysis (RDA) in vegan to eDNA metabarcoding community matrices (e.g. flower-surface arthropod OTU/ASV tables from COI/16S amplicons) to test whether biological communities are constrained by a categorical factor such as plant species, after removing geographic covariates (latitude/longitude) via Condition().
skills.when_to_use_negative: The community matrix is not sample-by-taxon (e.g. only a taxon list or abundance summary without matching metadata) — ordination requires the full matrix plus per-sample species/covariate annotations. The analysis question is unconstrained pattern description of community structure without a categorical hypothesis variable — an unconstrained ordination (PCA/PCoA/NMDS) is then more appropriate than RDA with Condition(). Metadata lack geographic covariates or there is no covariate to condition on, making a partial RDA (Condition(latitude, longitude)) mismatched to the design.

skills.description: Use when a raw eDNA amplicon OTU count table includes PCR replicate-level detections and suspected contaminant or sporadically detected OTUs must be removed via a site-occupancy occurrence-probability filter before taxonomic grouping.
skills.name: contaminant-otu-removal
skills.search_text: contaminant-otu-removal Use when a raw eDNA amplicon OTU count table includes PCR replicate-level detections and suspected contaminant or sporadically detected OTUs must be removed via a site-occupancy occurrence-probability filter before taxonomic grouping. The OTU table has no PCR replicate structure — without sample-by-replicate detections the binomial/site-occupancy occurrence probability cannot be estimated. Input is already taxonomically grouped (e.g., the 663 Family-or-higher groups) or is a post-filter sequence set; this QC step operates on raw OTU counts before grouping. Data are shotgun metagenomes or other non-replicated amplicon calls rather than PCR-replicated eDNA amplicon detections, where the replicate-based occurrence model does not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_3366 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A site-occupancy-based decontamination QC filter for eDNA amplicon data: PCR replicate detections are treated as independent binomial draws to estimate each OTU's occurrence probability, and OTUs with <80% estimated occurrence probability are eliminated. This 'removal of negatives' step ensures only reproducibly detected taxa feed taxonomic grouping and downstream community analysis. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-14105-1
skills.summary: A site-occupancy-based decontamination QC filter for eDNA amplicon data: PCR replicate detections are treated as independent binomial draws to estimate each OTU's occurrence probability, and OTUs with <80% estimated occurrence probability are eliminated. This 'removal of negatives' step ensures only reproducibly detected taxa feed taxonomic grouping and downstream community analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The OTU table has no PCR replicate structure — without sample-by-replicate detections the binomial/site-occupancy occurrence probability cannot be estimated. Input is already taxonomically grouped (e.g., the 663 Family-or-higher groups) or is a post-filter sequence set; this QC step operates on raw OTU counts before grouping. Data are shotgun metagenomes or other non-replicated amplicon calls rather than PCR-replicated eDNA amplicon detections, where the replicate-based occurrence model does not apply.

skills.description: Use when processing amplicon HTS metabarcoding data (FASTQ, ASV occurrence tables) that include negative controls and/or mock samples, and you need data-driven filter cutoffs instead of arbitrary read-count thresholds.
skills.name: control-based-filter-parameter-optimization
skills.search_text: control-based-filter-parameter-optimization Use when processing amplicon HTS metabarcoding data (FASTQ, ASV occurrence tables) that include negative controls and/or mock samples, and you need data-driven filter cutoffs instead of arbitrary read-count thresholds. The dataset has no negative controls or mock samples, since VTAM's parametrization depends explicitly on control samples to minimize FN and FP You only need generic denoising/clustering of sequencing errors (Swarm, Unoise, Deblur, DADA2) without control-driven filter threshold optimization Input is already a curated, filter-thresholded ASV table rather than raw occurrences with read counts per replicate http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Explicitly process negative control and mock community samples (with technical replicates) to determine optimal metabarcoding filtering parameter settings — e.g. VTAM's lfn_read_count_cutoff, lfn_sample_replicate_cutoff, lfn_variant_cutoff and pcr_error_var_prop — that minimize both false negatives (FN) and false positives (FP). metabarcoding/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.01.034
skills.summary: Explicitly process negative control and mock community samples (with technical replicates) to determine optimal metabarcoding filtering parameter settings — e.g. VTAM's lfn_read_count_cutoff, lfn_sample_replicate_cutoff, lfn_variant_cutoff and pcr_error_var_prop — that minimize both false negatives (FN) and false positives (FP).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has no negative controls or mock samples, since VTAM's parametrization depends explicitly on control samples to minimize FN and FP You only need generic denoising/clustering of sequencing errors (Swarm, Unoise, Deblur, DADA2) without control-driven filter threshold optimization Input is already a curated, filter-thresholded ASV table rather than raw occurrences with read counts per replicate

skills.description: Use when demultiplexed, merged ASV occurrence tables are available together with mock samples and negative controls, and you need to determine read-count or variant cut-offs that minimize false positives while retaining true positives.
skills.name: control-sample-false-positive-quantification
skills.search_text: control-sample-false-positive-quantification Use when demultiplexed, merged ASV occurrence tables are available together with mock samples and negative controls, and you need to determine read-count or variant cut-offs that minimize false positives while retaining true positives. Input is a single-sample dataset without mock community samples or negative controls, since the optimization explicitly requires control samples to identify false positives The data have already been filtered with optimized parameters and only downstream taxonomic assignment (taxassign) is needed Non-metabarcoding amplicon data where replicate structure and control samples are absent, so lfn/replicate-based cut-offs cannot be estimated http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Quantifies false positives in metabarcoding data using mock community and negative control samples to derive optimal filtering parameters (e.g. lfn_read_count_cutoff) per dataset with VTAM's optimize command. metabarcoding/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.01.034
skills.summary: Quantifies false positives in metabarcoding data using mock community and negative control samples to derive optimal filtering parameters (e.g. lfn_read_count_cutoff) per dataset with VTAM's optimize command.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a single-sample dataset without mock community samples or negative controls, since the optimization explicitly requires control samples to identify false positives The data have already been filtered with optimized parameters and only downstream taxonomic assignment (taxassign) is needed Non-metabarcoding amplicon data where replicate structure and control samples are absent, so lfn/replicate-based cut-offs cannot be estimated

skills.description: Use when you have per-habitat bespoke-weight species-level error rates and per-habitat weighted reference distributions, and want to test whether the confusion index predicts those error rates (target: Pearson r2 = 0.72, P = 1.4e-4).
skills.name: correlation-analysis-of-error-rates
skills.search_text: correlation-analysis-of-error-rates Use when you have per-habitat bespoke-weight species-level error rates and per-habitat weighted reference distributions, and want to test whether the confusion index predicts those error rates (target: Pearson r2 = 0.72, P = 1.4e-4). You are still generating or selecting taxonomic weights (use q2-clawback/readytowear weights directly) rather than explaining the error rates of weights you already have Input is raw per-sample or per-sequence classification output instead of aggregated per-habitat error rates — you must first aggregate species-level errors per habitat before fitting the correlation The sample habitats lack sufficiently characterized bespoke weights (e.g., natural sample types with insufficient Qiita/EMP characterization), so no per-habitat error rates or weighted distributions exist to correlate http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Quantifies how much of the species-level classification error rate of bespoke (clawback) taxonomic weights is explained by the confusion index — the log expected taxonomic distance between closely similar (k-mer Bray-Curtis < 0.25) sequences from different species in the same habitat — by fitting a linear regression of per-habitat error rate on confusion index. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12669-6
skills.summary: Quantifies how much of the species-level classification error rate of bespoke (clawback) taxonomic weights is explained by the confusion index — the log expected taxonomic distance between closely similar (k-mer Bray-Curtis < 0.25) sequences from different species in the same habitat — by fitting a linear regression of per-habitat error rate on confusion index.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You are still generating or selecting taxonomic weights (use q2-clawback/readytowear weights directly) rather than explaining the error rates of weights you already have Input is raw per-sample or per-sequence classification output instead of aggregated per-habitat error rates — you must first aggregate species-level errors per habitat before fitting the correlation The sample habitats lack sufficiently characterized bespoke weights (e.g., natural sample types with insufficient Qiita/EMP characterization), so no per-habitat error rates or weighted distributions exist to correlate

skills.description: Use when profiler outputs report taxa at finer or coarser ranks than genus/species and per-pairing genus- and species-level sensitivity/specificity must be benchmarked.
skills.name: count-matrix-aggregation-to-taxon-levels
skills.search_text: count-matrix-aggregation-to-taxon-levels Use when profiler outputs report taxa at finer or coarser ranks than genus/species and per-pairing genus- and species-level sensitivity/specificity must be benchmarked. Input is already collapsed to the target rank (e.g. an OTU/ASV table already aggregated to genus), so re-tracing the hierarchy would double-count or misassign reads The goal is amplicon sequence variant inference or read preprocessing rather than benchmarking taxon-level classification output Ground-truth composition tables for the samples are unavailable, since sensitivity and specificity cannot be computed without them http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Collapses profiler taxon count matrices (from DADA2, QIIME 2, Mothur, PathoScope 2, Kraken 2) to genus-level and species-level rows so detection sensitivity and assignment specificity can be computed against mock community ground truth. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-023-40799-x
skills.summary: Collapses profiler taxon count matrices (from DADA2, QIIME 2, Mothur, PathoScope 2, Kraken 2) to genus-level and species-level rows so detection sensitivity and assignment specificity can be computed against mock community ground truth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already collapsed to the target rank (e.g. an OTU/ASV table already aggregated to genus), so re-tracing the hierarchy would double-count or misassign reads The goal is amplicon sequence variant inference or read preprocessing rather than benchmarking taxon-level classification output Ground-truth composition tables for the samples are unavailable, since sensitivity and specificity cannot be computed without them

skills.description: Use when comparing code quality between two or more C++ codebase versions, or when validating that a refactoring/warning-fix campaign measurably improved static code quality.
skills.name: cpp-static-code-quality-analysis
skills.search_text: cpp-static-code-quality-analysis Use when comparing code quality between two or more C++ codebase versions, or when validating that a refactoring/warning-fix campaign measurably improved static code quality. The goal is functional/regression testing of behaviour rather than static code quality — the swarm project ships 806 black-box tests via the frederic-mahe/swarm-tests suite for that purpose The source tree is not C++ or the comparison targets are not distinct tagged versions, so the version-over-version score comparison is meaningless Quantify the static code quality of C++ source trees across software versions using SoftWipe (Zapletal et al., 2020), which computes a global code quality score out of 10. Used in the swarm v3 paper (DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab493) to demonstrate that v3's modernized C++ source code raised the score from 5.2 (swarm v2) to 6.6 (swarm v3). metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab493
skills.summary: Quantify the static code quality of C++ source trees across software versions using SoftWipe (Zapletal et al., 2020), which computes a global code quality score out of 10. Used in the swarm v3 paper (DOI 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab493) to demonstrate that v3's modernized C++ source code raised the score from 5.2 (swarm v2) to 6.6 (swarm v3).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is functional/regression testing of behaviour rather than static code quality — the swarm project ships 806 black-box tests via the frederic-mahe/swarm-tests suite for that purpose The source tree is not C++ or the comparison targets are not distinct tagged versions, so the version-over-version score comparison is meaningless

skills.description: Use when comparing computational cost of microbiome differential abundance methods on synthetic OTU tables with large taxon counts (e.g., 500 or 1000 taxa), where runtime differences of minutes vs hours are a decision factor.
skills.name: cpu-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cpu-runtime-benchmarking Use when comparing computational cost of microbiome differential abundance methods on synthetic OTU tables with large taxon counts (e.g., 500 or 1000 taxa), where runtime differences of minutes vs hours are a decision factor. The goal is statistical performance assessment (FDR control, power, p-values) rather than computational cost — use the paper's power/FDR simulation workflow instead The number of taxa is small enough that runtime is trivially fast for all methods and the benchmark cannot discriminate Input is real experimental data (e.g., the dietswap or global gut microbiota datasets) — this skill benchmarks on synthetic OTU tables, not empirical DA analysis Benchmarking methodology for measuring and comparing CPU runtime of differential abundance methods (ANCOM-BC vs ANCOM) on synthetic OTU count tables with large numbers of taxa (500 and 1000). It quantifies the computational cost gap that motivated ANCOM-BC's E-M based design over ANCOM's permutation-based log-ratio testing. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17041-7
skills.summary: Benchmarking methodology for measuring and comparing CPU runtime of differential abundance methods (ANCOM-BC vs ANCOM) on synthetic OTU count tables with large numbers of taxa (500 and 1000). It quantifies the computational cost gap that motivated ANCOM-BC's E-M based design over ANCOM's permutation-based log-ratio testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is statistical performance assessment (FDR control, power, p-values) rather than computational cost — use the paper's power/FDR simulation workflow instead The number of taxa is small enough that runtime is trivially fast for all methods and the benchmark cannot discriminate Input is real experimental data (e.g., the dietswap or global gut microbiota datasets) — this skill benchmarks on synthetic OTU tables, not empirical DA analysis

skills.description: Use when differential abundance results exist for the same phenotype across multiple independent datasets (e.g., five diarrhea or five obesity studies) and you need to quantify which DA tools call the same genera significant more often than expected by chance.
skills.name: cross-dataset-consistency-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-consistency-analysis Use when differential abundance results exist for the same phenotype across multiple independent datasets (e.g., five diarrhea or five obesity studies) and you need to quantify which DA tools call the same genera significant more often than expected by chance. The datasets span different environments/phenotypes where consistency could reflect technical or biological factors rather than shared signal — the article cautions that 'not all environments and datasets are appropriate for this comparison' (in the obesity group most tools were no better than chance). The goal is false-positive rate estimation under randomized group labels rather than cross-study consistency — use run_all_FP_datasets_filt.sh / run_all_FP_datasets_unfilt.sh instead of the consistency drivers. Only one dataset is available per phenotype, so there is no cross-study overlap to count; use within-dataset consensus/intersect of tool outputs instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Quantifies how consistently a differential abundance tool calls the same genera significant across multiple independent datasets of one phenotype (five diarrhea or five obesity 16S rRNA datasets), comparing observed cross-study overlap against a permutation-based random expectation and reporting observed/expected fold differences (e.g., ALDEx2 1.353-fold, p<0.001 in diarrhea). metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-28034-z
skills.summary: Quantifies how consistently a differential abundance tool calls the same genera significant across multiple independent datasets of one phenotype (five diarrhea or five obesity 16S rRNA datasets), comparing observed cross-study overlap against a permutation-based random expectation and reporting observed/expected fold differences (e.g., ALDEx2 1.353-fold, p<0.001 in diarrhea).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The datasets span different environments/phenotypes where consistency could reflect technical or biological factors rather than shared signal — the article cautions that 'not all environments and datasets are appropriate for this comparison' (in the obesity group most tools were no better than chance). The goal is false-positive rate estimation under randomized group labels rather than cross-study consistency — use run_all_FP_datasets_filt.sh / run_all_FP_datasets_unfilt.sh instead of the consistency drivers. Only one dataset is available per phenotype, so there is no cross-study overlap to count; use within-dataset consensus/intersect of tool outputs instead.

skills.description: Use when a study claims a new reference/training set improves on a predecessor, and the improvement must be verified by comparing taxonomic breadth (unique genera/taxa) and reference sequence counts parsed from the sets' taxonomy and FASTA files.
skills.name: cross-dataset-taxonomic-coverage-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-dataset-taxonomic-coverage-comparison Use when a study claims a new reference/training set improves on a predecessor, and the improvement must be verified by comparing taxonomic breadth (unique genera/taxa) and reference sequence counts parsed from the sets' taxonomy and FASTA files. The goal is to actually classify query CO1 sequences with the RDP classifier rather than benchmark training set composition The comparison targets classification accuracy metrics (e.g., leave-one-out correctness, false positive rates) rather than taxonomic coverage and sequence counts Only one training set is available, so no ratio-based comparison can be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Quantitatively benchmarks two taxonomic classifier training sets (e.g., the 2016 CO1 Eukaryote v1 set vs. the 2013 Insecta Genbank-Genus set) by counting unique taxa at a chosen rank and total reference sequences, then computing coverage and sequence ratios to verify claims like 'more than three times the taxonomic coverage... and almost five times as many reference sequences'. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-018-22505-4
skills.summary: Quantitatively benchmarks two taxonomic classifier training sets (e.g., the 2016 CO1 Eukaryote v1 set vs. the 2013 Insecta Genbank-Genus set) by counting unique taxa at a chosen rank and total reference sequences, then computing coverage and sequence ratios to verify claims like 'more than three times the taxonomic coverage... and almost five times as many reference sequences'.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to actually classify query CO1 sequences with the RDP classifier rather than benchmark training set composition The comparison targets classification accuracy metrics (e.g., leave-one-out correctness, false positive rates) rather than taxonomic coverage and sequence counts Only one training set is available, so no ratio-based comparison can be computed

skills.description: Use when comparing two profiler versions' fraction of explainable (classified) reads over the same metagenomic sample collection grouped by environment, e.g. benchmarking MetaPhlAn 4 vs MetaPhlAn 3.0.12 across >24,500 samples.
skills.name: cross-environment-read-explainability-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-environment-read-explainability-comparison Use when comparing two profiler versions' fraction of explainable (classified) reads over the same metagenomic sample collection grouped by environment, e.g. benchmarking MetaPhlAn 4 vs MetaPhlAn 3.0.12 across >24,500 samples. The input is functional profiling data (e.g. HUMAnN UniRef90/UniRef50 annotations) rather than taxonomic read-explainability comparison Only one profiler version is being run — there is no baseline (e.g. MetaPhlAn 3.0.12) to compute a fold increase against The goal is strain-level population genomics (StrainPhlAn) rather than comparing classified-read fractions across environments http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Quantifies how much more of the shotgun metagenomic read content a newer profiler (MetaPhlAn 4, with its 26,970 SGB / 4,992 uSGB marker database and unclassified-reads estimation) can explain relative to a previous version (MetaPhlAn 3.0.12) across host environments such as human gut, airways, wild mice, rumen, and ocean. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41587-023-01688-w
skills.summary: Quantifies how much more of the shotgun metagenomic read content a newer profiler (MetaPhlAn 4, with its 26,970 SGB / 4,992 uSGB marker database and unclassified-reads estimation) can explain relative to a previous version (MetaPhlAn 3.0.12) across host environments such as human gut, airways, wild mice, rumen, and ocean.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is functional profiling data (e.g. HUMAnN UniRef90/UniRef50 annotations) rather than taxonomic read-explainability comparison Only one profiler version is being run — there is no baseline (e.g. MetaPhlAn 3.0.12) to compute a fold increase against The goal is strain-level population genomics (StrainPhlAn) rather than comparing classified-read fractions across environments

skills.description: Use when eDNA metabarcoding data were generated with two (or more) marker primer sets, e.g. 16S rRNA and COI, and you must report per-marker taxonomic diversity, overlap (set intersection), and marker-specific recoveries.
skills.name: cross-marker-taxonomic-overlap-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-marker-taxonomic-overlap-analysis Use when eDNA metabarcoding data were generated with two (or more) marker primer sets, e.g. 16S rRNA and COI, and you must report per-marker taxonomic diversity, overlap (set intersection), and marker-specific recoveries. The dataset contains only one marker — there is no second marker table to intersect with, so a cross-marker overlap comparison is not applicable Input is raw sequencing reads or per-read taxonomy rather than MOTU-level family assignment tables — first collapse to one row per MOTU with its family before applying this comparison The comparison targets species- or community-composition clustering (e.g. clustering of arthropod communities by plant species) rather than counting family-level recovery per marker Quantifies how arthropod taxonomic recovery differs between two metabarcoding markers (mitochondrial 16S rRNA vs COI) by comparing per-MOTU family assignment tables, counting unique, shared, and marker-specific families, and checking mock-community recoveries per marker. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.4809
skills.summary: Quantifies how arthropod taxonomic recovery differs between two metabarcoding markers (mitochondrial 16S rRNA vs COI) by comparing per-MOTU family assignment tables, counting unique, shared, and marker-specific families, and checking mock-community recoveries per marker.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset contains only one marker — there is no second marker table to intersect with, so a cross-marker overlap comparison is not applicable Input is raw sequencing reads or per-read taxonomy rather than MOTU-level family assignment tables — first collapse to one row per MOTU with its family before applying this comparison The comparison targets species- or community-composition clustering (e.g. clustering of arthropod communities by plant species) rather than counting family-level recovery per marker

skills.description: Use when comparing 16S-derived genus/species abundance profiles (full-length V1–V9 or partial V1–V3 amplicons) against matched mWGS species abundances for the same samples, to judge whether a 16S region/platform combination achieves species-level resolution.
skills.name: cross-platform-16s-vs-mwgs-concordance-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-platform-16s-vs-mwgs-concordance-analysis Use when comparing 16S-derived genus/species abundance profiles (full-length V1–V9 or partial V1–V3 amplicons) against matched mWGS species abundances for the same samples, to judge whether a 16S region/platform combination achieves species-level resolution. The goal is strain-level discrimination via phasing of 16S gene SNPs/substitution profiles rather than OTU-based species abundance estimation Only one sequencing platform is available and no matched mWGS data exist, so no cross-platform concordance can be assessed Input data are already clustered OTU tables or abundance profiles rather than raw preprocessed amplicon read sets http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Quantifies Bacteroides genus- and species-level abundances from 99%-identity OTU clustering of full-length (V1–V9, PacBio) and partial (V1–V3, MiSeq) 16S amplicons and assesses their concordance with matched metagenomic whole-genome-shotgun (mWGS) quantification in the same stool samples. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-13036-1
skills.summary: Quantifies Bacteroides genus- and species-level abundances from 99%-identity OTU clustering of full-length (V1–V9, PacBio) and partial (V1–V3, MiSeq) 16S amplicons and assesses their concordance with matched metagenomic whole-genome-shotgun (mWGS) quantification in the same stool samples.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is strain-level discrimination via phasing of 16S gene SNPs/substitution profiles rather than OTU-based species abundance estimation Only one sequencing platform is available and no matched mWGS data exist, so no cross-platform concordance can be assessed Input data are already clustered OTU tables or abundance profiles rather than raw preprocessed amplicon read sets

skills.description: Use when an analysis requires isolating one or more source studies from a combined multi-project microbiome alpha diversity table, guided by project-code annotations (e.g., Table S3 codes) present in the sample metadata.
skills.name: cross-project-cohort-subsetting-by-metadata
skills.search_text: cross-project-cohort-subsetting-by-metadata Use when an analysis requires isolating one or more source studies from a combined multi-project microbiome alpha diversity table, guided by project-code annotations (e.g., Table S3 codes) present in the sample metadata. The input is a single-dataset alpha table (alpha-out_dataset-name.tsv) for one project only — no cross-project subsetting is needed The goal is a global correlation analysis (Supplementary Fig. S5) across all 4,596 samples, where subsetting would discard data The target projects lack associated metadata, since the paper excluded projects lacking metadata http://edamontology.org/topic_3337 Extracts specific study cohorts (e.g., projects coded 471_swedish and 514_imp_project) from the paper's aggregated alpha diversity tables (alpha_aggregated.tsv / alpha-out_dataset-name.tsv) using Table S3 project codes in the sample metadata, enabling per-project comparisons such as the Fig. 4 boxplots of Shannon, Observed features, and Berger-Parker. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-024-77864-y
skills.summary: Extracts specific study cohorts (e.g., projects coded 471_swedish and 514_imp_project) from the paper's aggregated alpha diversity tables (alpha_aggregated.tsv / alpha-out_dataset-name.tsv) using Table S3 project codes in the sample metadata, enabling per-project comparisons such as the Fig. 4 boxplots of Shannon, Observed features, and Berger-Parker.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a single-dataset alpha table (alpha-out_dataset-name.tsv) for one project only — no cross-project subsetting is needed The goal is a global correlation analysis (Supplementary Fig. S5) across all 4,596 samples, where subsetting would discard data The target projects lack associated metadata, since the paper excluded projects lacking metadata

skills.description: Use when building or validating a marker-specific eDNA reference database (e.g. for a 127-bp COI metabarcoding assay) and you must confirm your combined fasta matches a published reference release in sequence content and taxonomic coverage.
skills.name: cross-release-reference-database-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-release-reference-database-comparison Use when building or validating a marker-specific eDNA reference database (e.g. for a 127-bp COI metabarcoding assay) and you must confirm your combined fasta matches a published reference release in sequence content and taxonomic coverage. Your input is already a MOTU/feature table or reads needing taxonomic assignment — use ecotag against the finished database instead of rebuilding it Your metabarcoding marker is not the 127 bp elasmobranch COI fragment (e.g. a longer COI fragment or 12S) — the BOLD fragment filter and 120–135 bp size window are specific to this primer pair You only need non-elasmobranch off-target sequences and already have a validated combined release from github.com/metabarpark/Reference-databases to download http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Assembles a bespoke elasmobranch COI reference database (BOLD elasmobranch sequences plus ecoPCR-extracted non-elasmobranch homologs) and validates it by checking sequence content and taxonomic coverage against the published fasta release deposited at github.com/metabarpark/Reference-databases. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-017-17150-2
skills.summary: Assembles a bespoke elasmobranch COI reference database (BOLD elasmobranch sequences plus ecoPCR-extracted non-elasmobranch homologs) and validates it by checking sequence content and taxonomic coverage against the published fasta release deposited at github.com/metabarpark/Reference-databases.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is already a MOTU/feature table or reads needing taxonomic assignment — use ecotag against the finished database instead of rebuilding it Your metabarcoding marker is not the 127 bp elasmobranch COI fragment (e.g. a longer COI fragment or 12S) — the BOLD fragment filter and 120–135 bp size window are specific to this primer pair You only need non-elasmobranch off-target sequences and already have a validated combined release from github.com/metabarpark/Reference-databases to download

skills.description: Use when the same set of samples was sequenced or classified in two independent runs and you need to measure how reproducible OTU assignments and abundances are across runs.
skills.name: cross-run-abundance-correlation-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-run-abundance-correlation-analysis Use when the same set of samples was sequenced or classified in two independent runs and you need to measure how reproducible OTU assignments and abundances are across runs. Input is already a single-run dataset with no replicate/second-run sequencing — there is no cross-run pairing to correlate You need taxonomy-level abundance reproducibility rather than OTU-level (hierarchical OTU mappings) identification overlap Reads are raw and not demultiplexed/quality filtered — MAPseq expects previously demultiplexed and quality-filtered FASTA input http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Quantifies sequencing-run reproducibility of OTU-level abundance profiles by computing Spearman correlations of shared-OTU abundances and per-sample Jaccard indices of shared OTU identifications between two independent runs of the same samples, as done for the 2194-sample Human Microbiome Project dataset benchmarked against MAPseq, VSEARCH, NINJA-OPS, and USEARCH. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btx517
skills.summary: Quantifies sequencing-run reproducibility of OTU-level abundance profiles by computing Spearman correlations of shared-OTU abundances and per-sample Jaccard indices of shared OTU identifications between two independent runs of the same samples, as done for the 2194-sample Human Microbiome Project dataset benchmarked against MAPseq, VSEARCH, NINJA-OPS, and USEARCH.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single-run dataset with no replicate/second-run sequencing — there is no cross-run pairing to correlate You need taxonomy-level abundance reproducibility rather than OTU-level (hierarchical OTU mappings) identification overlap Reads are raw and not demultiplexed/quality filtered — MAPseq expects previously demultiplexed and quality-filtered FASTA input

skills.description: Use when shotgun metagenomes from related hosts (e.g. mother-infant pairs, household cohabitants) have been profiled with MetaPhlAn and you need to determine whether the same strain of a species — including uncharacterized uSGBs like Lachnospiraceae SGB4894 — is shared between samples.
skills.name: cross-sample-strain-tracking
skills.search_text: cross-sample-strain-tracking Use when shotgun metagenomes from related hosts (e.g. mother-infant pairs, household cohabitants) have been profiled with MetaPhlAn and you need to determine whether the same strain of a species — including uncharacterized uSGBs like Lachnospiraceae SGB4894 — is shared between samples. The target species lacks sufficiently many species-specific markers detected across samples (no reliable consensus marker sequence can be built, so strain clustering would be spurious). The question is species-level presence/absence or relative abundance profiling rather than strain-level resolution — MetaPhlAn 4 profiling alone suffices. Samples come from environmental or under-characterized habitats where current uSGBs fail to capture the sequences, per the article's discussion of profiling limitations. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Tracks individual microbial strains across host samples by reconstructing strain-level phylogenies from species-specific marker alignments with StrainPhlAn (available within MetaPhlAn), enabling inference of strain sharing and transmission (e.g. mother-to-infant vertical transmission) between hosts. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41587-023-01688-w
skills.summary: Tracks individual microbial strains across host samples by reconstructing strain-level phylogenies from species-specific marker alignments with StrainPhlAn (available within MetaPhlAn), enabling inference of strain sharing and transmission (e.g. mother-to-infant vertical transmission) between hosts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The target species lacks sufficiently many species-specific markers detected across samples (no reliable consensus marker sequence can be built, so strain clustering would be spurious). The question is species-level presence/absence or relative abundance profiling rather than strain-level resolution — MetaPhlAn 4 profiling alone suffices. Samples come from environmental or under-characterized habitats where current uSGBs fail to capture the sequences, per the article's discussion of profiling limitations.

skills.description: Use when you have per-dataset, per-tool significant-feature result tables and need to measure how much different DA tools agree (or disagree) on which ASVs are significantly differentially abundant, including under different prevalence-filtering regimes.
skills.name: cross-tool-jaccard-distance-computation
skills.search_text: cross-tool-jaccard-distance-computation Use when you have per-dataset, per-tool significant-feature result tables and need to measure how much different DA tools agree (or disagree) on which ASVs are significantly differentially abundant, including under different prevalence-filtering regimes. The goal is cross-study consistency (same tool across datasets from the same environment, e.g. the obesity or diarrhea consistency analyses) rather than cross-tool agreement within a dataset Only one differential abundance tool has been run, so there are no per-tool significant-ASV sets to compare pairwise The question is absolute accuracy or false positive rate of a tool; that requires the randomized false-positive analysis (run_all_FP_datasets_filt.sh / run_all_FP_datasets_unfilt.sh), not Jaccard overlap Quantifies agreement between differential abundance tools by computing pairwise Jaccard distances between the significant-ASV sets each tool reports per dataset (here 14 tools on 38 filtered and 38 unfiltered 16S rRNA datasets), then ordinating the mean distance matrix by PCoA to reveal tool clustering behavior. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-022-28034-z
skills.summary: Quantifies agreement between differential abundance tools by computing pairwise Jaccard distances between the significant-ASV sets each tool reports per dataset (here 14 tools on 38 filtered and 38 unfiltered 16S rRNA datasets), then ordinating the mean distance matrix by PCoA to reveal tool clustering behavior.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is cross-study consistency (same tool across datasets from the same environment, e.g. the obesity or diarrhea consistency analyses) rather than cross-tool agreement within a dataset Only one differential abundance tool has been run, so there are no per-tool significant-ASV sets to compare pairwise The question is absolute accuracy or false positive rate of a tool; that requires the randomized false-positive analysis (run_all_FP_datasets_filt.sh / run_all_FP_datasets_unfilt.sh), not Jaccard overlap

skills.description: Use when selecting a FASTQ preprocessing or QC tool on speed grounds: you must benchmark wall-clock time and reads/s of fastp vs FASTQC, Cutadapt, SOAPnuke, AfterQC and Trimmomatic in SE and PE modes on identical input, all single-threaded.

skills.search_text: cross-tool-performance-comparison Use when selecting a FASTQ preprocessing or QC tool on speed grounds: you must benchmark wall-clock time and reads/s of fastp vs FASTQC, Cutadapt, SOAPnuke, AfterQC and Trimmomatic in SE and PE modes on identical input, all single-threaded. Input is long-read data (Nanopore/PacBio) — fastp targets short reads (Illumina NovaSeq, MGI); fastplong is the long-read counterpart, so this comparison does not apply The goal is to compare trimming output quality or accuracy rather than speed — timing alone cannot judge cleaner reads Runs would be multi-threaded or use different input files — this breaks the single-threaded, identical-input like-for-like design of the benchmark http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Benchmarking skill for FASTQ preprocessing: measure wall-clock processing time and throughput (reads/s) of fastp, FASTQC, Cutadapt, SOAPnuke, AfterQC and Trimmomatic run single-threaded in SE and PE modes on one identical paired-end dataset (B17NCB1, 9316 M bases). It reproduces the paper's Table 1-style comparison showing fastp is 2-5 times faster than tools such as Trimmomatic or Cutadapt. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty560

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how much faster (and more memory-frugal) one sequence-analysis tool is than baselines on the same input, e.g. validating MAPseq's ~10x vs NINJA-OPS and ~100x vs VSEARCH speedups.
skills.name: cross-tool-speedup-ratio-computation
skills.search_text: cross-tool-speedup-ratio-computation Use when you need to quantify how much faster (and more memory-frugal) one sequence-analysis tool is than baselines on the same input, e.g. validating MAPseq's ~10x vs NINJA-OPS and ~100x vs VSEARCH speedups. Input is shotgun metagenomic data rather than amplicon rRNA reads — the reported 10x/100x ratios are specific to amplicon benchmarks (Fig. 1a) You need accuracy (F½-score) comparisons rather than runtime/memory benchmarking The baseline tools cannot be run on the identical input under the same profiling wrapper, making ratios non-comparable http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Benchmark MAPseq against competing rRNA analysis tools (NINJA-OPS, VSEARCH, USEARCH) on identical amplicon input, recording wall-clock runtime and peak memory to compute order-of-magnitude speedup ratios that reproduce the paper's Fig. 1a-b claims. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btx517
skills.summary: Benchmark MAPseq against competing rRNA analysis tools (NINJA-OPS, VSEARCH, USEARCH) on identical amplicon input, recording wall-clock runtime and peak memory to compute order-of-magnitude speedup ratios that reproduce the paper's Fig. 1a-b claims.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is shotgun metagenomic data rather than amplicon rRNA reads — the reported 10x/100x ratios are specific to amplicon benchmarks (Fig. 1a) You need accuracy (F½-score) comparisons rather than runtime/memory benchmarking The baseline tools cannot be run on the identical input under the same profiling wrapper, making ratios non-comparable

skills.description: Use when you have metabarcoding OTU tables (e.g. ITS2) paired with an independent species inventory (field survey lists) and need to measure whether curation (LULU, singleton removal, dbotu3) changes species-level composition.
skills.name: curated-otu-table-quality-metrics
skills.search_text: curated-otu-table-quality-metrics Use when you have metabarcoding OTU tables (e.g. ITS2) paired with an independent species inventory (field survey lists) and need to measure whether curation (LULU, singleton removal, dbotu3) changes species-level composition. There is no paired ground-truth species inventory (e.g. field survey list) to validate the OTU-derived inventories against The goal is alpha/beta diversity or taxonomic composition per se rather than assessing whether curation changed species-level fidelity relative to a survey The OTUs cannot be assigned to species because reference databases lack ITS2 (or equivalent marker) data for the taxa Quantifies how LULU post-clustering curation changes per-site taxonomic composition of OTU tables by classifying OTU-derived species against paired vascular plant field survey lists as recaptured, imperfect reference matches, unregistered, redundant, or lost recaptured species. Provides the validation logic (Table 2) for judging whether curation improves species-level fidelity. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-017-01312-x
skills.summary: Quantifies how LULU post-clustering curation changes per-site taxonomic composition of OTU tables by classifying OTU-derived species against paired vascular plant field survey lists as recaptured, imperfect reference matches, unregistered, redundant, or lost recaptured species. Provides the validation logic (Table 2) for judging whether curation improves species-level fidelity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: There is no paired ground-truth species inventory (e.g. field survey list) to validate the OTU-derived inventories against The goal is alpha/beta diversity or taxonomic composition per se rather than assessing whether curation changed species-level fidelity relative to a survey The OTUs cannot be assigned to species because reference databases lack ITS2 (or equivalent marker) data for the taxa

skills.description: Use when a resolved species list from eDNA metabarcoding (e.g., the 93 Vestamager-resolved arthropod taxa) needs independent validation against public occurrence records at defined geographic levels before ecological interpretation.
skills.name: danish-fauna-geographic-concordance-analysis
skills.search_text: danish-fauna-geographic-concordance-analysis Use when a resolved species list from eDNA metabarcoding (e.g., the 93 Vestamager-resolved arthropod taxa) needs independent validation against public occurrence records at defined geographic levels before ecological interpretation. The taxon list contains only unassigned or higher-level (family/order) OTUs rather than species-level assignments, which cannot be matched against species-level faunistic records. The study area lies outside Danish/database coverage such that Naturbasen and Fauna Europaea cannot provide meaningful presence/absence evidence for the sampled locality. The goal is to test primer or sequencing performance rather than ecological plausibility of an already-resolved species list. Validates eDNA-resolved arthropod taxa against independent Danish faunistic occurrence databases (Naturbasen / allearter, Fauna Europaea) by flagging each species as present or absent at a specific locality (Vestamager) and region (Amager), then tallying concordance percentages as an ecological plausibility check on metabarcoding results. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.4809
skills.summary: Validates eDNA-resolved arthropod taxa against independent Danish faunistic occurrence databases (Naturbasen / allearter, Fauna Europaea) by flagging each species as present or absent at a specific locality (Vestamager) and region (Amager), then tallying concordance percentages as an ecological plausibility check on metabarcoding results.

skills.search_text: database-sample-mismatch-detection Use when analyzing long-read (PacBio/ONT) metagenomic samples against RefSeq and you suspect out-of-database contaminants (e.g. eukaryotic genomes) or database-sample mismatches detectable via identity and coverage patterns. Samples dominated by short reads, which fall below the minimum length needed for reliable minimizer-based mapping and remain unassigned Complex samples comprising many non-characterized entities where no single contaminant or mismatch signal dominates Analyses requiring real-time/streaming classification during sequencing, which MetaMaps does not support http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Detect incongruities between a metagenomic sample and the reference database using MetaMaps' per-read mapping output: out-of-database large genomes remain unclassified with high precision, while in-database but mismatched samples reveal themselves via shifted estimated-alignment-identity distributions and uneven read-depth coverage along reference contigs. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-10934-2
