skills.search_text: high-memory-benchmark-monitoring Use when you need to quantify runtime and memory requirements of a multi-sample amplicon workflow (e.g. >27,000 samples, billions of reads) on a bounded cluster allocation such as 50 cores. Input is already a processed feature/ASV table and no raw-read preprocessing will be run, so there is nothing to benchmark The dataset is small enough (e.g. a few samples on a laptop) that bigmem node requirements and cluster core limits are irrelevant You only need interactive exploratory analysis rather than a reproducible scalability measurement against a reference footprint (87 h / 190 GB / 50 cores) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A benchmarking skill for measuring wall-clock runtime and peak memory of large-scale amplicon processing: it reproduces the dadasnake/DADA2 pipeline on the Earth Microbiome Project scale (2.1 billion reads, >27,000 samples) on ≤50 CPU cores to characterize computational footprint (~87 real hours, >190 GB RAM). metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giaa135
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for measuring wall-clock runtime and peak memory of large-scale amplicon processing: it reproduces the dadasnake/DADA2 pipeline on the Earth Microbiome Project scale (2.1 billion reads, >27,000 samples) on ≤50 CPU cores to characterize computational footprint (~87 real hours, >190 GB RAM).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a processed feature/ASV table and no raw-read preprocessing will be run, so there is nothing to benchmark The dataset is small enough (e.g. a few samples on a laptop) that bigmem node requirements and cluster core limits are irrelevant You only need interactive exploratory analysis rather than a reproducible scalability measurement against a reference footprint (87 h / 190 GB / 50 cores)

skills.description: Use when comparing runtime speed and memory footprint of two versions of a clustering/bioinformatics tool on very large (10.6M-sequence) FASTA inputs, and when output equivalence must be verified between versions.
skills.name: high-throughput-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: high-throughput-runtime-benchmarking Use when comparing runtime speed and memory footprint of two versions of a clustering/bioinformatics tool on very large (10.6M-sequence) FASTA inputs, and when output equivalence must be verified between versions. Input is a raw FASTQ or non-dereplicated FASTA — swarm strictly requires dereplicated input with abundance values in the sequence headers (e.g., _1000 suffixes) The goal is to compare clustering quality under different d thresholds rather than to benchmark runtime and memory between tool versions Datasets are small — speedup and memory ratios measured on tera-scale inputs (10.6M amplicons) do not necessarily transfer to small files http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Benchmark a new release of a high-throughput tool (swarm v3) against its predecessor (swarm v2) on million-scale dereplicated amplicon datasets, measuring wall-clock runtime and peak resident memory under 1-core and 16-core conditions while verifying that clustering output is identical. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btab493
skills.summary: Benchmark a new release of a high-throughput tool (swarm v3) against its predecessor (swarm v2) on million-scale dereplicated amplicon datasets, measuring wall-clock runtime and peak resident memory under 1-core and 16-core conditions while verifying that clustering output is identical.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw FASTQ or non-dereplicated FASTA — swarm strictly requires dereplicated input with abundance values in the sequence headers (e.g., _1000 suffixes) The goal is to compare clustering quality under different d thresholds rather than to benchmark runtime and memory between tool versions Datasets are small — speedup and memory ratios measured on tera-scale inputs (10.6M amplicons) do not necessarily transfer to small files

skills.description: Use when comparing per-sample alpha diversity across metabarcoding feature tables generated by different denoising or clustering pipelines, or when quantifying how stringency of sequence filtering changes diversity estimates.
skills.name: hill-numbers-alpha-diversity-estimation
skills.search_text: hill-numbers-alpha-diversity-estimation Use when comparing per-sample alpha diversity across metabarcoding feature tables generated by different denoising or clustering pipelines, or when quantifying how stringency of sequence filtering changes diversity estimates. Input is already a single-denominator beta diversity or ordination result — this skill is specifically about per-sample alpha estimates on rarefied tables Samples cannot be rarefied to the 5,000-read depth because they fall below the standard filter's ≥5,000 total filtered reads threshold The question is taxonomic classifier accuracy rather than diversity metric sensitivity — use the classifier benchmarking workflows of this study instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3305 Compute Hill Numbers (order 0 = observed richness, 1 = Shannon's Entropy, 2 = Simpson's Index) per bat guano sample from rarefied COI feature tables using Phyloseq/Vegan in R, then test whether denoising program (DADA2, Deblur, VSEARCH) and filtering regime significantly alter these alpha diversity estimates. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.6594
skills.summary: Compute Hill Numbers (order 0 = observed richness, 1 = Shannon's Entropy, 2 = Simpson's Index) per bat guano sample from rarefied COI feature tables using Phyloseq/Vegan in R, then test whether denoising program (DADA2, Deblur, VSEARCH) and filtering regime significantly alter these alpha diversity estimates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single-denominator beta diversity or ordination result — this skill is specifically about per-sample alpha estimates on rarefied tables Samples cannot be rarefied to the 5,000-read depth because they fall below the standard filter's ≥5,000 total filtered reads threshold The question is taxonomic classifier accuracy rather than diversity metric sensitivity — use the classifier benchmarking workflows of this study instead

skills.description: Use when analysis input consists of HMP-derived 16S rRNA OTU datasets (V1V3 or V3V5 hypervariable regions) clustered at 97% sequence similarity, and per-OTU representative-to-member sequence relationships must be loaded for dissimilarity (MSD/BLD) computations or regional comparisons.
skills.name: hmp-16s-otu-dataset-handling
skills.search_text: hmp-16s-otu-dataset-handling Use when analysis input consists of HMP-derived 16S rRNA OTU datasets (V1V3 or V3V5 hypervariable regions) clustered at 97% sequence similarity, and per-OTU representative-to-member sequence relationships must be loaded for dissimilarity (MSD/BLD) computations or regional comparisons. Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) or an amplicon dataset not yet clustered into OTUs — this skill operates on already-clustered HMP OTU datasets, not upstream clustering itself. Input is a feature table or abundance data where per-sequence representative-member relationships are absent; MSD/BLD read-to-representative pairing cannot be constructed. Analysis concerns taxonomic annotation of representative sequences rather than quantitative dissimilarity handling — the annotation step is a separate workflow. http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3300 Handles the HMP V1V3 and V3V5 16S rRNA OTU datasets generated by QIIME with a 97% percent-sequence-similarity (PSD) threshold, organizing read-to-representative pairwise MSD and BLD dissimilarities for downstream metric comparisons. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/npjbiofilms.2016.4
skills.summary: Handles the HMP V1V3 and V3V5 16S rRNA OTU datasets generated by QIIME with a 97% percent-sequence-similarity (PSD) threshold, organizing read-to-representative pairwise MSD and BLD dissimilarities for downstream metric comparisons.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (FASTQ) or an amplicon dataset not yet clustered into OTUs — this skill operates on already-clustered HMP OTU datasets, not upstream clustering itself. Analysis concerns taxonomic annotation of representative sequences rather than quantitative dissimilarity handling — the annotation step is a separate workflow.

skills.description: Use when OTUs were clustered with PSD at a 97% sequence similarity threshold from 16S amplicon data (V1V3 or V3V5) and you need to re-measure their compactness with MSD/BLD per taxonomic group and per region.
skills.name: hmp-amplicon-region-comparison
skills.search_text: hmp-amplicon-region-comparison Use when OTUs were clustered with PSD at a 97% sequence similarity threshold from 16S amplicon data (V1V3 or V3V5) and you need to re-measure their compactness with MSD/BLD per taxonomic group and per region. Input OTUs were not clustered with percent sequence dissimilarity (PSD) at the ~97% threshold — the compactness re-measurement is specifically designed to audit PSD-97% OTUs. The analysis goal is end-to-end community profiling (abundance tables, beta diversity) rather than auditing OTU cluster quality via representative-to-member dissimilarity. Sequences lack taxonomic assignments, since the per-taxon aggregation (TM7, Cyanobacteria, Lactobacillus, Staphylococcus, Sneathia) requires annotated OTU members. http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 Quantifies OTU compactness by computing MSD (mean sequence dissimilarity) and BLD (branch length distance) between each HMP V1V3/V3V5 OTU representative and its member sequences, then aggregates per-taxon mean metrics across the two 16S hypervariable regions. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/npjbiofilms.2016.4
skills.summary: Quantifies OTU compactness by computing MSD (mean sequence dissimilarity) and BLD (branch length distance) between each HMP V1V3/V3V5 OTU representative and its member sequences, then aggregates per-taxon mean metrics across the two 16S hypervariable regions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input OTUs were not clustered with percent sequence dissimilarity (PSD) at the ~97% threshold — the compactness re-measurement is specifically designed to audit PSD-97% OTUs. The analysis goal is end-to-end community profiling (abundance tables, beta diversity) rather than auditing OTU cluster quality via representative-to-member dissimilarity. Sequences lack taxonomic assignments, since the per-taxon aggregation (TM7, Cyanobacteria, Lactobacillus, Staphylococcus, Sneathia) requires annotated OTU members.

skills.description: Use when analyzing PacBio CCS read-to-reference alignments of full-length 16S amplicons to quantify whether deletion errors coincide with homopolymer runs, or to explain why highly similar 16S copies cannot be resolved.
skills.name: homopolymer-deletion-coincidence-analysis
skills.search_text: homopolymer-deletion-coincidence-analysis Use when analyzing PacBio CCS read-to-reference alignments of full-length 16S amplicons to quantify whether deletion errors coincide with homopolymer runs, or to explain why highly similar 16S copies cannot be resolved. Input reads are Illumina short-read data of 16S variable regions rather than PacBio CCS full-length amplicons The analysis goal is substitution-based discrimination of intragenomic 16S copies where indels are deliberately ignored (the article's filter step focuses on substitutions and ignores insertions/deletions) No reference 16S sequences are available, so deletion positions cannot be mapped to homopolymer context http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Characterizes systematic deletion errors in PacBio CCS full-length 16S reads by mapping every alignment deletion to its reference position and testing overlap with homopolymer runs (>=4 identical consecutive bases) in the 16S reference sequences, as in Supplementary Figs. 6-7 of Johnson et al. 2019. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-13036-1
skills.summary: Characterizes systematic deletion errors in PacBio CCS full-length 16S reads by mapping every alignment deletion to its reference position and testing overlap with homopolymer runs (>=4 identical consecutive bases) in the 16S reference sequences, as in Supplementary Figs. 6-7 of Johnson et al. 2019.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are Illumina short-read data of 16S variable regions rather than PacBio CCS full-length amplicons The analysis goal is substitution-based discrimination of intragenomic 16S copies where indels are deliberately ignored (the article's filter step focuses on substitutions and ignores insertions/deletions) No reference 16S sequences are available, so deletion positions cannot be mapped to homopolymer context

skills.description: Use when raw metagenomic FASTQ files must be cleaned of host-contaminating reads before taxonomic (MetaPhlAn2, Kraken2) or functional (HUMAnN2) profiling.

skills.search_text: iterative-likelihood-convergence-monitoring Use when probabilistic per-read mapping scores span multiple candidate (and possibly closely related) reference genomes and you must simultaneously estimate overall sample composition and disambiguate ambiguous read-to-genome assignments. The sample has a high proportion of short reads — minimizer-based mapping yields unreliable mapping locations below the minimum read length, so EM posteriors are poorly grounded The sample comprises many non-characterized entities absent from the database — EM convergence will not detect missing taxa, and database-sample mismatches require separate visual or automatic thresholding of coverage/identity patterns You only need a fast k-mer taxonomic label without composition estimation or per-read positional output — k-mer tools (Kraken2, CLARK, MetaOthello) may suffice, though they can suffer false positives from large contaminant genomes http://edamontology.org/topic_0659 Applies the Expectation-Maximization algorithm to iteratively re-estimate the sample composition vector F from composition-weighted read posteriors, using convergence of the total data likelihood as the stopping criterion, and resolves each ambiguous read to its maximum-likelihood genome under the converged composition. In MetaMaps this is what turns mapping-quality-based probabilities over >12,000 RefSeq genomes into both composition estimates and per-read taxonomic assignments. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-10934-2

skills.description: Use when per-sample alpha diversity indices (Shannon, inverse Simpson, Chao1) computed from a genus-level ASV abundance table must be compared across discrete groups, such as samples grouped by the 16S rRNA hypervariable region amplified, to test whether one region has significantly lower diversity.

skills.search_text: l1-distance-compositional-comparison Use when benchmarking metagenomic classification/composition-estimation tools against known sample ground truth, and you need a per-tool, per-dataset L1-distance metric between estimated and true taxonomic abundance profiles. Sample genomes or close relatives are not in the reference database, since database-sample mismatch invalidates the composition comparison (as discussed for HMP7 and CAMI) The sample contains a high proportion of short reads or many non-characterized entities, which MetaMaps and this benchmarking design do not handle well http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Quantify the accuracy of metagenomic sample-composition estimates by computing the L1 distance between tool-estimated taxonomic abundance profiles and ground-truth compositions, alongside Pearson r2, for long-read metagenomic classifiers such as MetaMaps on the i100, p25, CAMI, HMP7, and Zymo datasets. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-10934-2
skills.summary: Quantify the accuracy of metagenomic sample-composition estimates by computing the L1 distance between tool-estimated taxonomic abundance profiles and ground-truth compositions, alongside Pearson r2, for long-read metagenomic classifiers such as MetaMaps on the i100, p25, CAMI, HMP7, and Zymo datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sample genomes or close relatives are not in the reference database, since database-sample mismatch invalidates the composition comparison (as discussed for HMP7 and CAMI) The sample contains a high proportion of short reads or many non-characterized entities, which MetaMaps and this benchmarking design do not handle well

skills.description: Use when per-sample alpha-diversity (e.g. observed richness) must be summarized against an environmental gradient (pH, temperature) to locate the gradient value at which the 99th-percentile richness peaks, using a peaked, two-sided exponential rather than a Gaussian.
skills.name: laplace-curve-fitting-nonlinear-least-squares
skills.search_text: laplace-curve-fitting-nonlinear-least-squares Use when per-sample alpha-diversity (e.g. observed richness) must be summarized against an environmental gradient (pH, temperature) to locate the gradient value at which the 99th-percentile richness peaks, using a peaked, two-sided exponential rather than a Gaussian. The metadata lacks the environmental variable of interest (e.g. no pH or temperature values), since binning and peak location cannot be computed You need mean/typical richness along the gradient rather than the upper bound — the 99th-percentile binning targets the maximum-observed richness envelope The feature table has not passed the mc2 minimum-sequence-count filter (count ≥ 2), which the article's workflow applies before computing richness http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Fits a two-sided exponential (Laplace) model, richness = a*exp(-|x-x0|/b), to binned richness-vs-gradient data (pH, temperature) from the EMP 16S Release 1 dataset using scipy curve_fit, and benchmarks it against a Gaussian fit to justify the Laplace shape. This recovers the pH/temperature locations of peak microbial richness. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/nature24621
skills.summary: Fits a two-sided exponential (Laplace) model, richness = a*exp(-|x-x0|/b), to binned richness-vs-gradient data (pH, temperature) from the EMP 16S Release 1 dataset using scipy curve_fit, and benchmarks it against a Gaussian fit to justify the Laplace shape. This recovers the pH/temperature locations of peak microbial richness.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The metadata lacks the environmental variable of interest (e.g. no pH or temperature values), since binning and peak location cannot be computed You need mean/typical richness along the gradient rather than the upper bound — the 99th-percentile binning targets the maximum-observed richness envelope The feature table has not passed the mc2 minimum-sequence-count filter (count ≥ 2), which the article's workflow applies before computing richness

skills.description: Use when dereplicated ASV/OTU sequences from 16S, 18S, ITS, or COI amplicon data need reference-based taxonomic labels before downstream diversity or mock-community benchmarking.
skills.name: last-common-ancestor-taxonomy-assignment
skills.search_text: last-common-ancestor-taxonomy-assignment Use when dereplicated ASV/OTU sequences from 16S, 18S, ITS, or COI amplicon data need reference-based taxonomic labels before downstream diversity or mock-community benchmarking. Input is raw .fastq.gz reads — taxonomy assignment must come after pre-processing, chimera removal, and clustering/ASV inference COI MOTUs where the target taxa may be absent from MIDORI (e.g. no entry for B. leachii in MIDORI_LONGEST_1.1) Analyses requiring a phylogeny-based placement that goes beyond the alignment-based LCA approach — for 16S rRNA only, prefer PEMA's phylogeny-based assignment with SILVA_132_SSURef, EPA-ng and RaxML-ng http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Assign taxonomy to ASV/OTU sequences from eDNA metabarcoding using the CREST LCAClassifier against the Silva reference database for 16S/18S rRNA marker genes, with Unite for ITS and MIDORI/RDPClassifier for COI. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giaa022
skills.summary: Assign taxonomy to ASV/OTU sequences from eDNA metabarcoding using the CREST LCAClassifier against the Silva reference database for 16S/18S rRNA marker genes, with Unite for ITS and MIDORI/RDPClassifier for COI.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw .fastq.gz reads — taxonomy assignment must come after pre-processing, chimera removal, and clustering/ASV inference COI MOTUs where the target taxa may be absent from MIDORI (e.g. no entry for B. leachii in MIDORI_LONGEST_1.1) Analyses requiring a phylogeny-based placement that goes beyond the alignment-based LCA approach — for 16S rRNA only, prefer PEMA's phylogeny-based assignment with SILVA_132_SSURef, EPA-ng and RaxML-ng

skills.description: Use when a genus-level ASV abundance table split into predefined classes (e.g., hypervariable region combinations) must be screened for differentially abundant taxa and ranked as biomarkers by LDA effect size.
skills.name: lda-effect-size-biomarker-ranking
skills.search_text: lda-effect-size-biomarker-ranking Use when a genus-level ASV abundance table split into predefined classes (e.g., hypervariable region combinations) must be screened for differentially abundant taxa and ranked as biomarkers by LDA effect size. Input is raw reads or full-length 16S rRNA sequence data rather than a collapsed genus-level abundance table with predefined sample classes The analysis goal is overall diversity or ordination (e.g., alpha diversity by Kruskal–Wallis, NMDS of Bray–Curtis dissimilarities) rather than group-discriminating taxa No meaningful class variable exists — LEfSe requires predefined groups (e.g., region combinations) to estimate between-class effect sizes http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Runs LEfSe on Greengenes-collapsed, genus-level 16S rRNA ASV abundance tables to rank discriminant bacterial genera per sample group (here, combined hypervariable regions V1–V2, V3–V4, V5–V7, V7–V9) using log10-transformed LDA scores with a threshold > 2. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-023-30764-z
skills.summary: Runs LEfSe on Greengenes-collapsed, genus-level 16S rRNA ASV abundance tables to rank discriminant bacterial genera per sample group (here, combined hypervariable regions V1–V2, V3–V4, V5–V7, V7–V9) using log10-transformed LDA scores with a threshold > 2.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw reads or full-length 16S rRNA sequence data rather than a collapsed genus-level abundance table with predefined sample classes The analysis goal is overall diversity or ordination (e.g., alpha diversity by Kruskal–Wallis, NMDS of Bray–Curtis dissimilarities) rather than group-discriminating taxa No meaningful class variable exists — LEfSe requires predefined groups (e.g., region combinations) to estimate between-class effect sizes

skills.description: Use when merging taxonomic labels from multiple identical or near-identical COI reference records, or when classifier output provides multiple hits without coverage metadata and a conservative single lineage per sequence is needed.
skills.name: least-common-ancestor-taxonomy-resolution
skills.search_text: least-common-ancestor-taxonomy-resolution Use when merging taxonomic labels from multiple identical or near-identical COI reference records, or when classifier output provides multiple hits without coverage metadata and a conservative single lineage per sequence is needed. When each reference sequence already carries a single, complete, non-redundant lineage (e.g., a curated RDP-formatted training set) — consensus collapsing adds no information. When the goal is maximal species-level resolution rather than a conservative assignment — LCA will truncate to the deepest rank at which all member taxonomies agree. When headers or classifier hits lack comparable rank-delimited taxonomy strings, since the consensus script cannot reconcile incompatible lineage formats. http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Applies an LCA / consensus-taxonomy approach to resolve taxonomic strings for dereplicated COI reference sequences (e.g., Porter GenBank-derived records clustered at 100% identity) and to classify metabarcoding hits (e.g., BOLD API results lacking query coverage), yielding a single consensus lineage per sequence or cluster. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.6594
skills.summary: Applies an LCA / consensus-taxonomy approach to resolve taxonomic strings for dereplicated COI reference sequences (e.g., Porter GenBank-derived records clustered at 100% identity) and to classify metabarcoding hits (e.g., BOLD API results lacking query coverage), yielding a single consensus lineage per sequence or cluster.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When each reference sequence already carries a single, complete, non-redundant lineage (e.g., a curated RDP-formatted training set) — consensus collapsing adds no information. When the goal is maximal species-level resolution rather than a conservative assignment — LCA will truncate to the deepest rank at which all member taxonomies agree. When headers or classifier hits lack comparable rank-delimited taxonomy strings, since the consensus script cannot reconcile incompatible lineage formats.

skills.description: Use when you need to measure how much bespoke (source-environment) taxonomic weights matter, by benchmarking mis-matched or 'deliberately incorrect' habitat weights against uniform weights across habitat classes.
skills.name: leave-one-habitat-out-classification-benchmark
skills.search_text: leave-one-habitat-out-classification-benchmark Use when you need to measure how much bespoke (source-environment) taxonomic weights matter, by benchmarking mis-matched or 'deliberately incorrect' habitat weights against uniform weights across habitat classes. Your query samples already have a bespoke weight set for their true source habitat — apply the correct bespoke weights directly rather than benchmarking mis-matched weights Your samples come from habitats not represented in the weight inventory (e.g. highly unusual distributions like synthetic populations), where no cross-habitat weight assembly is possible You only need genus-level classification, where the equal-abundance assumption's impact is much smaller than at species level http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A benchmark that quantifies how species-level naive Bayes classification degrades when class weights from the wrong habitat are applied: for each of 14 EMPO 3 habitats, samples are classified with q2-clawback weights from each of the other 13 habitats plus a uniform-weights control, and error rates are regressed against weight divergence. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12669-6
skills.summary: A benchmark that quantifies how species-level naive Bayes classification degrades when class weights from the wrong habitat are applied: for each of 14 EMPO 3 habitats, samples are classified with q2-clawback weights from each of the other 13 habitats plus a uniform-weights control, and error rates are regressed against weight divergence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your query samples already have a bespoke weight set for their true source habitat — apply the correct bespoke weights directly rather than benchmarking mis-matched weights Your samples come from habitats not represented in the weight inventory (e.g. highly unusual distributions like synthetic populations), where no cross-habitat weight assembly is possible You only need genus-level classification, where the equal-abundance assumption's impact is much smaller than at species level

skills.description: Use when a Naive Bayes/RDP-style metabarcode classifier needs rank- and fragment-length-specific bootstrap support cutoffs, or when the minimum confidence threshold guaranteeing ~99% correct CO1 assignments must be established before applying it to metabarcode queries.
skills.name: leave-one-out-classifier-validation
skills.search_text: leave-one-out-classifier-validation Use when a Naive Bayes/RDP-style metabarcode classifier needs rank- and fragment-length-specific bootstrap support cutoffs, or when the minimum confidence threshold guaranteeing ~99% correct CO1 assignments must be established before applying it to metabarcode queries. Queries may contain taxa not represented in the reference training set — the classifier is not meant to classify unrepresented taxa, so leave-one-out cutoffs would overstate real-world accuracy Species-rank assignments with the genus-trained CO1 Eukaryote v1 set — Table 2 reports N/A (no cutoff achieves 99% correct assignments at species rank) A different training-set version (e.g. v5.1.0) with its own 5-fold cross-validation cutoffs is already published — reusing these v1 leave-one-out cutoffs would mix incompatible thresholds (v3 README lists 40% genus at 500 bp+, v5.1.0 lists 0.3) http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3050 Empirically calibrates taxonomic-assignment confidence cutoffs by running RDP classifier v2.12 leave-one-out tests over a CO1 reference training set (e.g. CO1 Eukaryote v1) across fragment lengths, then deriving the minimum bootstrap support cutoff per taxonomic rank that yields at least 99% correct assignments (Table 2). metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-018-22505-4
skills.summary: Empirically calibrates taxonomic-assignment confidence cutoffs by running RDP classifier v2.12 leave-one-out tests over a CO1 reference training set (e.g. CO1 Eukaryote v1) across fragment lengths, then deriving the minimum bootstrap support cutoff per taxonomic rank that yields at least 99% correct assignments (Table 2).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Queries may contain taxa not represented in the reference training set — the classifier is not meant to classify unrepresented taxa, so leave-one-out cutoffs would overstate real-world accuracy Species-rank assignments with the genus-trained CO1 Eukaryote v1 set — Table 2 reports N/A (no cutoff achieves 99% correct assignments at species rank) A different training-set version (e.g. v5.1.0) with its own 5-fold cross-validation cutoffs is already published — reusing these v1 leave-one-out cutoffs would mix incompatible thresholds (v3 README lists 40% genus at 500 bp+, v5.1.0 lists 0.3)

skills.description: Use when you have a genus-collapsed ASV abundance table grouped by experimental categories (e.g., 16S hypervariable region combinations) and need to identify taxa with significantly different relative abundances among groups.
skills.name: lefse-differential-abundance-analysis
skills.search_text: lefse-differential-abundance-analysis Use when you have a genus-collapsed ASV abundance table grouped by experimental categories (e.g., 16S hypervariable region combinations) and need to identify taxa with significantly different relative abundances among groups. The abundance table is not collapsed at genus level against Greengenes (or an equivalent reference), since the reported discriminant taxa and LDA threshold behavior are genus-level. You need to compare taxonomic profiles against full-length third-generation 16S rRNA sequencing — the study explicitly did not perform this comparison. The sample categories are not discrete groups (e.g., region combinations, phenotype labels); LEfSe's LDA-based class discrimination requires group labels. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Runs LEfSe discriminative analysis on genus-level 16S rRNA ASV abundance tables (Greengenes-collapsed, from sputum samples) grouped by combined hypervariable region (V1–V2, V3–V4, V5–V7, V7–V9) to assign biomarker genera per region via LDA scores. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-023-30764-z
skills.summary: Runs LEfSe discriminative analysis on genus-level 16S rRNA ASV abundance tables (Greengenes-collapsed, from sputum samples) grouped by combined hypervariable region (V1–V2, V3–V4, V5–V7, V7–V9) to assign biomarker genera per region via LDA scores.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The abundance table is not collapsed at genus level against Greengenes (or an equivalent reference), since the reported discriminant taxa and LDA threshold behavior are genus-level. You need to compare taxonomic profiles against full-length third-generation 16S rRNA sequencing — the study explicitly did not perform this comparison. The sample categories are not discrete groups (e.g., region combinations, phenotype labels); LEfSe's LDA-based class discrimination requires group labels.

skills.description: Use when a denoised or clustered mock-community feature table still contains unexpected mock ASVs ('miss' variants such as partial/miss ASVs) that the standard low-abundance filter did not remove, and you need an empirically derived per-library cutoff to zero them out.
skills.name: library-specific-artifact-count-scaling
skills.search_text: library-specific-artifact-count-scaling Use when a denoised or clustered mock-community feature table still contains unexpected mock ASVs ('miss' variants such as partial/miss ASVs) that the standard low-abundance filter did not remove, and you need an empirically derived per-library cutoff to zero them out. Input is raw reads or unfiltered output — this filter operates on an already-denoised/clustered ASV/OTU frequency table that has gone through the standard singleton-drop and ≥5,000-read filter first. There is no mock community in the dataset — the per-library subtraction integer is derived from observed 'miss' mock variant maxima and cannot be computed from diet samples alone. The goal is only the standard low-abundance filter; the extra per-library subtraction is a separate, more aggressive step for removing unexpected mock variants. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 An extra filtering step for mock-community ASV/OTU feature tables that combines a standard filter (drop singletons across the dataset, retain samples with ≥5,000 filtered reads) with a per-library subtraction of the maximum count observed for unexpected ('miss') mock variants, zeroing any negative or zero results. It empirically removes low-abundance unexpected sequences (partial and miss ASVs) that survive denoising/clustering. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.6594
skills.summary: An extra filtering step for mock-community ASV/OTU feature tables that combines a standard filter (drop singletons across the dataset, retain samples with ≥5,000 filtered reads) with a per-library subtraction of the maximum count observed for unexpected ('miss') mock variants, zeroing any negative or zero results. It empirically removes low-abundance unexpected sequences (partial and miss ASVs) that survive denoising/clustering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw reads or unfiltered output — this filter operates on an already-denoised/clustered ASV/OTU frequency table that has gone through the standard singleton-drop and ≥5,000-read filter first. There is no mock community in the dataset — the per-library subtraction integer is derived from observed 'miss' mock variant maxima and cannot be computed from diet samples alone. The goal is only the standard low-abundance filter; the extra per-library subtraction is a separate, more aggressive step for removing unexpected mock variants.

skills.description: Use when per-sample benchmark metrics (sensitivity, specificity, NRMSE, alpha diversity) are collected across multiple profiler/reference-library pairings on the same 136 mock community samples, and you need pairwise significance testing between pairings while accounting for sample-to-sample.
skills.name: linear-mixed-effects-model-fitting
skills.search_text: linear-mixed-effects-model-fitting Use when per-sample benchmark metrics (sensitivity, specificity, NRMSE, alpha diversity) are collected across multiple profiler/reference-library pairings on the same 136 mock community samples, and you need pairwise significance testing between pairings while accounting for sample-to-sample. The outcome is not a per-sample continuous metric with repeated measurements across pairings, so a random-intercept structure (1|sample) is inappropriate The data are count-based or binomial taxon detections that violate linear-model assumptions and would require a generalized mixed model rather than lmer() http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 Fits linear mixed-effects models with lme4::lmer() to compare taxonomic profiler/reference-library pairings on per-sample benchmark metrics from 136 mock community 16S samples, then uses lsmeans() with Tukey adjustment for all pairwise post hoc contrasts as reported in Supplementary Tables S2–S7. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-023-40799-x
skills.summary: Fits linear mixed-effects models with lme4::lmer() to compare taxonomic profiler/reference-library pairings on per-sample benchmark metrics from 136 mock community 16S samples, then uses lsmeans() with Tukey adjustment for all pairwise post hoc contrasts as reported in Supplementary Tables S2–S7.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The outcome is not a per-sample continuous metric with repeated measurements across pairings, so a random-intercept structure (1|sample) is inappropriate The data are count-based or binomial taxon detections that violate linear-model assumptions and would require a generalized mixed model rather than lmer()

skills.description: Use when a compositional taxon-by-sample abundance table (e.g., SGB-level MetaPhlAn 4 profiles) has repeated/host-structured metadata and the goal is per-taxon association testing with covariate control and FDR correction.
skills.name: linear-mixed-effects-modeling-of-microbiome-abundances
skills.search_text: linear-mixed-effects-modeling-of-microbiome-abundances Use when a compositional taxon-by-sample abundance table (e.g., SGB-level MetaPhlAn 4 profiles) has repeated/host-structured metadata and the goal is per-taxon association testing with covariate control and FDR correction. Input is raw sequencing reads rather than a taxon-by-sample abundance profile — profile first with MetaPhlAn 4 before modeling Samples lack the covariate structure (e.g., repeated measures, vendor/cohort batching) that motivates a random-intercept model; a simple fixed-effect regression would suffice Taxa below the ~1% mean relative abundance threshold dominate the question (e.g., rare-taxon detection), since sparse CLR-transformed bins lack power here http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Identifies taxonomic biomarkers (e.g., MetaPhlAn 4 SGBs) associated with a host condition by fitting a random-intercept linear mixed model per taxon on CLR-transformed abundances, covarying out host factors and controlling FDR. Used to show that uncharacterized species (uSGBs) dominate high-fat-diet biomarkers in mouse gut microbiomes. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41587-023-01688-w
skills.summary: Identifies taxonomic biomarkers (e.g., MetaPhlAn 4 SGBs) associated with a host condition by fitting a random-intercept linear mixed model per taxon on CLR-transformed abundances, covarying out host factors and controlling FDR. Used to show that uncharacterized species (uSGBs) dominate high-fat-diet biomarkers in mouse gut microbiomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads rather than a taxon-by-sample abundance profile — profile first with MetaPhlAn 4 before modeling Samples lack the covariate structure (e.g., repeated measures, vendor/cohort batching) that motivates a random-intercept model; a simple fixed-effect regression would suffice Taxa below the ~1% mean relative abundance threshold dominate the question (e.g., rare-taxon detection), since sparse CLR-transformed bins lack power here

skills.description: Use when per-location count data (e.g. MOTU richness or read abundances from metabarcoding) must be tested for significant differences among sampling locations, and pairwise location contrasts with P-values are needed.
skills.name: location-factor-categorical-modeling
skills.search_text: location-factor-categorical-modeling Use when per-location count data (e.g. MOTU richness or read abundances from metabarcoding) must be tested for significant differences among sampling locations, and pairwise location contrasts with P-values are needed. When the response variable is continuous and approximately normal rather than count data (Poisson GLM and square-root-transformed read counts are specific to this design) When the goal is taxonomic assignment or MOTU delimitation itself — this skill operates downstream on the already-constructed MOTU richness/abundance table When samples lack a categorical grouping factor (e.g. single-site time series), since location as a factor is the core of the model http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Fits generalized linear models with sampling location entered as a categorical factor to test whether MOTU richness and square-root-transformed eDNA read abundance differ among sites, followed by post-hoc Tukey pairwise contrasts (multcomp) to identify which locations differ. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-017-17150-2
skills.summary: Fits generalized linear models with sampling location entered as a categorical factor to test whether MOTU richness and square-root-transformed eDNA read abundance differ among sites, followed by post-hoc Tukey pairwise contrasts (multcomp) to identify which locations differ.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the response variable is continuous and approximately normal rather than count data (Poisson GLM and square-root-transformed read counts are specific to this design) When the goal is taxonomic assignment or MOTU delimitation itself — this skill operates downstream on the already-constructed MOTU richness/abundance table When samples lack a categorical grouping factor (e.g. single-site time series), since location as a factor is the core of the model

skills.description: Use when a paper reports species/OTU occurrence only as Venn-diagram segment counts across sampling sites or sources, and a machine-readable occurrence table must be reconstructed and validated.
skills.name: location-wise-shared-species-accounting
skills.search_text: location-wise-shared-species-accounting Use when a paper reports species/OTU occurrence only as Venn-diagram segment counts across sampling sites or sources, and a machine-readable occurrence table must be reconstructed and validated. The raw OTU/species abundance table or Venn source data is already available digitally — then extract counts directly instead of reconstructing them Relative-abundance or read-count data is needed rather than integer species-presence counts, since this skill reproduces occurrence (species) numbers only The paper reports continuous diversity metrics (e.g., Simpson index, Bray-Curtis distances) rather than discrete species segment counts http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Reconstructs a tidy species-occurrence table from published Venn-diagram counts, splitting bacterial species into inflow (I-source) and pond (P-source) per location (B, N, G) plus unique and shared segments. This lets downstream agents reuse species-level occurrence numbers without access to raw OTU tables. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-020-80236-x
skills.summary: Reconstructs a tidy species-occurrence table from published Venn-diagram counts, splitting bacterial species into inflow (I-source) and pond (P-source) per location (B, N, G) plus unique and shared segments. This lets downstream agents reuse species-level occurrence numbers without access to raw OTU tables.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The raw OTU/species abundance table or Venn source data is already available digitally — then extract counts directly instead of reconstructing them Relative-abundance or read-count data is needed rather than integer species-presence counts, since this skill reproduces occurrence (species) numbers only The paper reports continuous diversity metrics (e.g., Simpson index, Bray-Curtis distances) rather than discrete species segment counts

skills.description: Use when comparing the log ratio of two taxa (e.g., Bacteroidetes to Firmicutes) between groups such as US vs non-US subjects in compositional microbiome data, requiring bias-corrected mean differences, standard errors, and p-values.
skills.name: log-ratio-hypothesis-testing
skills.search_text: log-ratio-hypothesis-testing Use when comparing the log ratio of two taxa (e.g., Bacteroidetes to Firmicutes) between groups such as US vs non-US subjects in compositional microbiome data, requiring bias-corrected mean differences, standard errors, and p-values. Sample sizes are very small (e.g., n = 5 per group), where ANCOM-BC may not perform well and FDR is not controlled The taxon of interest is classified as a structural zero in a group (neg.lb = TRUE flags it), since ANCOM-BC is not designed to test differential abundance of structural zeros The group variable is not discrete, since ANCOM-BC v1.0 only supports discrete group.var http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Tests hypotheses about log-ratios of microbial taxon abundances between experimental groups using ANCOM-BC's bias-corrected linear regression framework, which estimates sample-specific sampling fractions to correct compositional bias before testing. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17041-7
skills.summary: Tests hypotheses about log-ratios of microbial taxon abundances between experimental groups using ANCOM-BC's bias-corrected linear regression framework, which estimates sample-specific sampling fractions to correct compositional bias before testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sample sizes are very small (e.g., n = 5 per group), where ANCOM-BC may not perform well and FDR is not controlled The taxon of interest is classified as a structural zero in a group (neg.lb = TRUE flags it), since ANCOM-BC is not designed to test differential abundance of structural zeros The group variable is not discrete, since ANCOM-BC v1.0 only supports discrete group.var

skills.description: Use when you need to estimate or verify the sample-specific offset (bias) term in ANCOM-BC's log-scale linear regression, i.e., reconstruct how bias.em and bias.wls arise from the taxa-level Delta_i mixture fit.
skills.name: log-scale-sampling-fraction-estimation
skills.search_text: log-scale-sampling-fraction-estimation Use when you need to estimate or verify the sample-specific offset (bias) term in ANCOM-BC's log-scale linear regression, i.e., reconstruct how bias.em and bias.wls arise from the taxa-level Delta_i mixture fit. The analysis goal is differential abundance calling itself (mean.difference, W, p.val, q.val) rather than reconstructing or inspecting the bias-offset estimation step Very small sample sizes (e.g., n = 5 per group), where ANCOM-BC may not perform well and FDR is not controlled Data have not been pre-processed (no structural-zero matrix or grp.ind available) — run feature_table_pre_process first http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Reconstructs ANCOM-BC's estimation of the sampling-fraction bias term: fitting a three-component Gaussian mixture to per-taxon log-scale mean differences via an E-M algorithm, and cross-checking with a weighted-least-squares variance approximation. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-17041-7
skills.summary: Reconstructs ANCOM-BC's estimation of the sampling-fraction bias term: fitting a three-component Gaussian mixture to per-taxon log-scale mean differences via an E-M algorithm, and cross-checking with a weighted-least-squares variance approximation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is differential abundance calling itself (mean.difference, W, p.val, q.val) rather than reconstructing or inspecting the bias-offset estimation step Very small sample sizes (e.g., n = 5 per group), where ANCOM-BC may not perform well and FDR is not controlled Data have not been pre-processed (no structural-zero matrix or grp.ind available) — run feature_table_pre_process first

skills.description: Use when empirical per-read pass-number distributions extracted from real PacBio HiFi runs (e.g. ATCC 16S Sequel II System 2.0 data) are sparse or noisy, and you need a fitted lognormal np distribution for read simulation.
skills.name: lognormal-distribution-fitting
skills.search_text: lognormal-distribution-fitting Use when empirical per-read pass-number distributions extracted from real PacBio HiFi runs (e.g. ATCC 16S Sequel II System 2.0 data) are sparse or noisy, and you need a fitted lognormal np distribution for read simulation. The empirical pass-number distribution from the real run is dense and smooth enough to use directly via --np-distribution (empirical mode) The simulator target is not PacBio HiFi amplicon data and pass number is not a meaningful read attribute You need to simulate Illumina or short-read data where PBSIM3 subread pass modeling does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Fits lognormal distributions to sparse or noisy empirical per-read pass-number distributions from PacBio HiFi runs, so that MHASS can sample a smooth number-of-passes (np) distribution to drive per-pass PBSIM3 subread simulation. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf656
skills.summary: Fits lognormal distributions to sparse or noisy empirical per-read pass-number distributions from PacBio HiFi runs, so that MHASS can sample a smooth number-of-passes (np) distribution to drive per-pass PBSIM3 subread simulation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The empirical pass-number distribution from the real run is dense and smooth enough to use directly via --np-distribution (empirical mode) The simulator target is not PacBio HiFi amplicon data and pass number is not a meaningful read attribute You need to simulate Illumina or short-read data where PBSIM3 subread pass modeling does not apply

skills.description: Use when validating that simulated HiFi amplicon reads reproduce the error (edit distance) distributions of real sequencing data for mock communities such as Zymo/Titan-1, ATCC/16S, or Phylotag/16S.
skills.name: long-read-amplicon-error-profiling
skills.search_text: long-read-amplicon-error-profiling Use when validating that simulated HiFi amplicon reads reproduce the error (edit distance) distributions of real sequencing data for mock communities such as Zymo/Titan-1, ATCC/16S, or Phylotag/16S. The goal is to simulate reads rather than profile errors of existing reads — use MHASS directly instead Input reads are short-read (Illumina) amplicon data; the error model and HiFi pass-number logic here target PacBio HiFi circular consensus reads Only a single genome/ASV is present, so a per-genome distribution comparison against real mock-community data is not meaningful http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Profiles per-genome edit-distance distributions of PacBio HiFi amplicon reads (simulated by MHASS or real) by computing the minimum Levenshtein distance from each read to candidate reference ASVs, enabling validation that simulated error profiles match real sequencing data across mock communities. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf656
skills.summary: Profiles per-genome edit-distance distributions of PacBio HiFi amplicon reads (simulated by MHASS or real) by computing the minimum Levenshtein distance from each read to candidate reference ASVs, enabling validation that simulated error profiles match real sequencing data across mock communities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to simulate reads rather than profile errors of existing reads — use MHASS directly instead Input reads are short-read (Illumina) amplicon data; the error model and HiFi pass-number logic here target PacBio HiFi circular consensus reads Only a single genome/ASV is present, so a per-genome distribution comparison against real mock-community data is not meaningful

skills.description: Use when calling within-genome 16S gene copy variants from full-length PacBio amplicon reads (e.g., B. vulgatus OTUs at 99% identity) and substitution frequencies must be separated from platform-specific indel errors.
skills.name: long-read-error-aware-variant-calling
skills.search_text: long-read-error-aware-variant-calling Use when calling within-genome 16S gene copy variants from full-length PacBio amplicon reads (e.g., B. vulgatus OTUs at 99% identity) and substitution frequencies must be separated from platform-specific indel errors. When the variants of interest are insertions or deletions — PacBio CCS deletion errors coincident with homopolymer runs make indel calls unreliable, and the paper notes a single real deletion in an E. coli K-12 MG1655 16S gene would be missed by this substitution-only approach When working with short-read 16S variable-region data (e.g., V4), which cannot resolve full-gene intragenomic copy variants When reads are not full-length 16S amplicons, since resolving divergent intragenomic copies requires sequencing the entire ~1500 bp gene http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Detects intragenomic 16S rRNA gene copy polymorphisms from full-length PacBio CCS amplicons by aligning reads to a reference with Cross_match and tabulating only nucleotide substitutions, deliberately ignoring insertions/deletions because systematic PacBio CCS deletion errors coincide with homopolymer runs. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-13036-1
skills.summary: Detects intragenomic 16S rRNA gene copy polymorphisms from full-length PacBio CCS amplicons by aligning reads to a reference with Cross_match and tabulating only nucleotide substitutions, deliberately ignoring insertions/deletions because systematic PacBio CCS deletion errors coincide with homopolymer runs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the variants of interest are insertions or deletions — PacBio CCS deletion errors coincident with homopolymer runs make indel calls unreliable, and the paper notes a single real deletion in an E. coli K-12 MG1655 16S gene would be missed by this substitution-only approach When working with short-read 16S variable-region data (e.g., V4), which cannot resolve full-gene intragenomic copy variants When reads are not full-length 16S amplicons, since resolving divergent intragenomic copies requires sequencing the entire ~1500 bp gene

skills.description: Use when you need strain-/species-level assignment and sample composition from long-read (PacBio/ONT) metagenomic FASTQ data, especially with reads ≥1000 bp and a comprehensive reference database.
skills.name: long-read-metagenomic-read-mapping
skills.search_text: long-read-metagenomic-read-mapping Use when you need strain-/species-level assignment and sample composition from long-read (PacBio/ONT) metagenomic FASTQ data, especially with reads ≥1000 bp and a comprehensive reference database. Samples dominated by short reads: reads below the minimum length (1000 bp) end up with minimizer sets too small to reliably determine mapping locations and remain unassigned Complex samples comprising many non-characterized entities not represented in the reference database Applications requiring real-time/streaming analysis — MetaMaps does not support streaming data http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 A two-stage skill for assigning long PacBio/Oxford Nanopore metagenomic reads: minimizer-based approximate mapping (MashMap-derived) against a comprehensive RefSeq database, followed by probabilistic scoring of mapping locations and EM-based sample composition estimation, yielding per-read locations, alignment identities, and mapping qualities. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-10934-2
skills.summary: A two-stage skill for assigning long PacBio/Oxford Nanopore metagenomic reads: minimizer-based approximate mapping (MashMap-derived) against a comprehensive RefSeq database, followed by probabilistic scoring of mapping locations and EM-based sample composition estimation, yielding per-read locations, alignment identities, and mapping qualities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Samples dominated by short reads: reads below the minimum length (1000 bp) end up with minimizer sets too small to reliably determine mapping locations and remain unassigned Complex samples comprising many non-characterized entities not represented in the reference database Applications requiring real-time/streaming analysis — MetaMaps does not support streaming data

skills.description: Use when full-length (~1500 bp) 16S PacBio CCS reads must be mapped to a single 16S reference to quantify per-position substitutions that distinguish intragenomic 16S gene copies within one genome.
skills.name: long-read-to-reference-alignment
skills.search_text: long-read-to-reference-alignment Use when full-length (~1500 bp) 16S PacBio CCS reads must be mapped to a single 16S reference to quantify per-position substitutions that distinguish intragenomic 16S gene copies within one genome. The goal is to resolve intragenomic 16S differences involving insertions or deletions — PacBio CCS deletion errors coincident with homopolymer runs, and a single deletion in one of the seven E. coli K-12 MG1655 16S genes, make the substitutions-only approach imperfect The input reads are short reads covering only partial 16S variable regions (e.g., V4), which the article shows cannot recapture the diversity of the full ~1500 bp gene http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Aligns full-length PacBio CCS 16S rRNA reads to a single reference 16S gene sequence and tallies per-position substitution frequencies to resolve intragenomic 16S copy variation (e.g., the seven 16S copies of E. coli K-12 MG1655). metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-13036-1
skills.summary: Aligns full-length PacBio CCS 16S rRNA reads to a single reference 16S gene sequence and tallies per-position substitution frequencies to resolve intragenomic 16S copy variation (e.g., the seven 16S copies of E. coli K-12 MG1655).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to resolve intragenomic 16S differences involving insertions or deletions — PacBio CCS deletion errors coincident with homopolymer runs, and a single deletion in one of the seven E. coli K-12 MG1655 16S genes, make the substitutions-only approach imperfect The input reads are short reads covering only partial 16S variable regions (e.g., V4), which the article shows cannot recapture the diversity of the full ~1500 bp gene

skills.description: Use when a QIIME 2 feature table generated from mock-community or diet metabarcoding reads contains unexpected ASVs and you need to assess how standard/extra low-abundance filtering changes per-method error rates.
skills.name: low-abundance-variant-filtering
skills.search_text: low-abundance-variant-filtering Use when a QIIME 2 feature table generated from mock-community or diet metabarcoding reads contains unexpected ASVs and you need to assess how standard/extra low-abundance filtering changes per-method error rates. Input is already a heavily filtered feature table where singletons and low-read samples have been removed — reapplying the standard filter changes nothing and the extra subtraction could distort true counts The study goal is to compare denoising programs' raw error profiles (e.g., unexpected ASV counts) without mitigation, since this skill's purpose is precisely to remove that signal Working with non-metabarcoding data lacking an expected-species reference, since the 'miss'-count subtraction in the extra filter is derived from mock community alignments http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 A post-denoising/clustering filtering strategy for COI metabarcoding feature tables in which low-abundance sequence variants (singletons and variants observed in few samples) are removed to mitigate the excess of unexpected (erroneous) ASVs produced by clustering methods like VSEARCH relative to denoisers like DADA2 and Deblur. metabarcoding/v1 10.1002/ece3.6594
skills.summary: A post-denoising/clustering filtering strategy for COI metabarcoding feature tables in which low-abundance sequence variants (singletons and variants observed in few samples) are removed to mitigate the excess of unexpected (erroneous) ASVs produced by clustering methods like VSEARCH relative to denoisers like DADA2 and Deblur.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a heavily filtered feature table where singletons and low-read samples have been removed — reapplying the standard filter changes nothing and the extra subtraction could distort true counts The study goal is to compare denoising programs' raw error profiles (e.g., unexpected ASV counts) without mitigation, since this skill's purpose is precisely to remove that signal Working with non-metabarcoding data lacking an expected-species reference, since the 'miss'-count subtraction in the extra filter is derived from mock community alignments

skills.description: Decision support for choosing and applying low-frequency-noise cutoffs (read count, per-sample-replicate abundance, per-variant abundance) to ASV occurrence tables during VTAM's filter step, especially when negative controls and replicates inform threshold optimization.
skills.name: low-frequency-noise-thresholding
skills.search_text: low-frequency-noise-thresholding Decision support for choosing and applying low-frequency-noise cutoffs (read count, per-sample-replicate abundance, per-variant abundance) to ASV occurrence tables during VTAM's filter step, especially when negative controls and replicates inform threshold optimization. The goal is filtering PCR errors via sequence similarity — VTAM's FilterPCRerror discards occurrences when an ASV closely matches another ASV with a significantly higher number of reads, which is a distinct filter from LFN thresholding. Input is raw FASTQ reads rather than an ASV occurrence table — reads must first go through VTAM's merge, sortreads, and filter steps before occurrence-level cutoffs apply. Cutoffs have not been optimized for the dataset at hand — the paper's values (60 reads, 0.002, 0.006) were optimized for the bat dataset and VTAM suggested different read-count cut-offs for other datasets (10 for fish, 40 for shark). http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Implements VTAM's FilterLNF (Filter Low Frequency Noise) step, which removes low-frequency ASV occurrences that likely reflect tag-jump, inter-sample contamination, or sequencing noise by applying three per-occurrence read-count and relative-abundance cutoffs. metabarcoding/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2023.01.034
skills.summary: Implements VTAM's FilterLNF (Filter Low Frequency Noise) step, which removes low-frequency ASV occurrences that likely reflect tag-jump, inter-sample contamination, or sequencing noise by applying three per-occurrence read-count and relative-abundance cutoffs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is filtering PCR errors via sequence similarity — VTAM's FilterPCRerror discards occurrences when an ASV closely matches another ASV with a significantly higher number of reads, which is a distinct filter from LFN thresholding. Input is raw FASTQ reads rather than an ASV occurrence table — reads must first go through VTAM's merge, sortreads, and filter steps before occurrence-level cutoffs apply. Cutoffs have not been optimized for the dataset at hand — the paper's values (60 reads, 0.002, 0.006) were optimized for the bat dataset and VTAM suggested different read-count cut-offs for other datasets (10 for fish, 40 for shark).

skills.description: Use when you have paired OTU tables (e.g. uncurated and LULU-curated variants) and an independent survey matrix over the same samples, and you need to test correlation of their dissimilarity matrices.
skills.name: mantel-correlation-testing
skills.search_text: mantel-correlation-testing Use when you have paired OTU tables (e.g. uncurated and LULU-curated variants) and an independent survey matrix over the same samples, and you need to test correlation of their dissimilarity matrices. The goal is validating alpha-diversity or species-level identity of individual OTUs — Mantel correlation only assesses matrix-level turnover/composition, not single rare species The OTU tables do not share a common sample set with the ground-truth survey data (Mantel requires paired, identically ordered samples) Only one OTU table is available with no uncurated/curated counterpart or external reference matrix to correlate against Runs Mantel tests (Pearson correlation with 999 permutations) between Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrices computed from uncurated vs LULU-curated OTU tables and against vascular plant field survey data, to quantify whether LULU post-clustering curation changes community dissimilarity and whether curation improves OTU-vs-ground-truth beta-diversity correlation. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-017-01312-x
skills.summary: Runs Mantel tests (Pearson correlation with 999 permutations) between Bray-Curtis dissimilarity matrices computed from uncurated vs LULU-curated OTU tables and against vascular plant field survey data, to quantify whether LULU post-clustering curation changes community dissimilarity and whether curation improves OTU-vs-ground-truth beta-diversity correlation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is validating alpha-diversity or species-level identity of individual OTUs — Mantel correlation only assesses matrix-level turnover/composition, not single rare species The OTU tables do not share a common sample set with the ground-truth survey data (Mantel requires paired, identically ordered samples) Only one OTU table is available with no uncurated/curated counterpart or external reference matrix to correlate against

skills.description: Use when a metabarcoding study reports an isolation-by-distance Mantel test and you must capture the correlation coefficient and p-value per sample type (e.g., inflow vs pond water) into a structured record.
skills.name: mantel-test-statistics-extraction
skills.search_text: mantel-test-statistics-extraction Use when a metabarcoding study reports an isolation-by-distance Mantel test and you must capture the correlation coefficient and p-value per sample type (e.g., inflow vs pond water) into a structured record. Input is raw sequencing reads or a FASTQ QC pipeline step — this skill only captures Mantel test statistics, not read processing The diversity metric of interest is eukaryotic/ITS beta-diversity — the article's Mantel test was computed on Bray-Curtis beta-diversity of prokaryotes only No geographic coordinate or distance information exists for the samples — the Mantel test requires an inter-farm distance matrix, and in this study exact farm locations were withheld http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Extracts and encodes Mantel test results correlating Bray-Curtis beta-diversity (prokaryotes only) with inter-farm geographic distance, preserving per-water-source significance outcomes (pond-water r = 0.969, p < 0.0001 vs inflow I-source p > 0.05). metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41598-020-80236-x
skills.summary: Extracts and encodes Mantel test results correlating Bray-Curtis beta-diversity (prokaryotes only) with inter-farm geographic distance, preserving per-water-source significance outcomes (pond-water r = 0.969, p < 0.0001 vs inflow I-source p > 0.05).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads or a FASTQ QC pipeline step — this skill only captures Mantel test statistics, not read processing The diversity metric of interest is eukaryotic/ITS beta-diversity — the article's Mantel test was computed on Bray-Curtis beta-diversity of prokaryotes only No geographic coordinate or distance information exists for the samples — the Mantel test requires an inter-farm distance matrix, and in this study exact farm locations were withheld

skills.description: Use when a long-read metagenomic mapper (MetaMaps after MashMap-style approximate mapping) has produced multiple candidate mapping locations per read and you need probabilistic per-location mapping qualities rather than a single hit.
skills.name: mapping-quality-posterior-normalization
skills.search_text: mapping-quality-posterior-normalization Use when a long-read metagenomic mapper (MetaMaps after MashMap-style approximate mapping) has produced multiple candidate mapping locations per read and you need probabilistic per-location mapping qualities rather than a single hit. The sample contains a high proportion of short reads — reads below the chosen minimum length end up with minimizer sets too small to reliably determine mapping locations You need exact base-to-base alignments rather than approximate mapping locations with probabilistic qualities (MashMap/MetaMaps do not compute alignments explicitly) The goal is pure k-mer-based taxonomic classification without positional mapping information (e.g. Kraken2-style pipelines) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Scores each candidate mapping location of a long read with MetaMaps' binomial model over shared minimizers (MinHash intersection size against union size, with success probability (1-e)^k), then normalizes the per-location scores into posterior mapping qualities that sum to 1 across all candidate locations of the read. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-10934-2
skills.summary: Scores each candidate mapping location of a long read with MetaMaps' binomial model over shared minimizers (MinHash intersection size against union size, with success probability (1-e)^k), then normalizes the per-location scores into posterior mapping qualities that sum to 1 across all candidate locations of the read.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample contains a high proportion of short reads — reads below the chosen minimum length end up with minimizer sets too small to reliably determine mapping locations You need exact base-to-base alignments rather than approximate mapping locations with probabilistic qualities (MashMap/MetaMaps do not compute alignments explicitly) The goal is pure k-mer-based taxonomic classification without positional mapping information (e.g. Kraken2-style pipelines)

skills.description: Use when comparing how well FASTQ reads filtered by different preprocessing tools align to a reference genome, and you need per-tool mapping metrics like mismatches, clips, and single-read maps.
skills.name: mapping-statistics-aggregation
skills.search_text: mapping-statistics-aggregation Use when comparing how well FASTQ reads filtered by different preprocessing tools align to a reference genome, and you need per-tool mapping metrics like mismatches, clips, and single-read maps. Input is long-read data (Nanopore, PacBio, Cyclone) — fastp/BWA-MEM on Illumina-style short reads does not apply; use fastplong instead The question is about preprocessing speed or QC report generation rather than downstream alignment quality comparison Only one preprocessing tool is available and no raw-data baseline exists — a relative ranking cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Aggregates BWA-MEM/Samtools alignment statistics (mapped bases, mismatched bases, soft/hard-clipped reads, single-read maps) for NS_PE150 FASTQ data preprocessed by different tools, to rank preprocessing quality against a raw-data baseline. metabarcoding/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/bty560
skills.summary: Aggregates BWA-MEM/Samtools alignment statistics (mapped bases, mismatched bases, soft/hard-clipped reads, single-read maps) for NS_PE150 FASTQ data preprocessed by different tools, to rank preprocessing quality against a raw-data baseline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is long-read data (Nanopore, PacBio, Cyclone) — fastp/BWA-MEM on Illumina-style short reads does not apply; use fastplong instead The question is about preprocessing speed or QC report generation rather than downstream alignment quality comparison Only one preprocessing tool is available and no raw-data baseline exists — a relative ranking cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when a chained community-network-analysis step has produced subnetwork membership/richness tables and you must test each subnetwork's association with measured environmental time-series such as SST or chlorophyll a.
skills.name: marine-environmental-time-series-analysis
skills.search_text: marine-environmental-time-series-analysis Use when a chained community-network-analysis step has produced subnetwork membership/richness tables and you must test each subnetwork's association with measured environmental time-series such as SST or chlorophyll a. Input is raw sequencing data or an unclustered feature table — the subnetwork membership must already exist from the upstream WGCNA community-network-analysis step Environmental variables and eDNA time points are not sample-aligned (no matched dates), since rank correlation requires paired observations The goal is inferring direct predator-prey interactions from co-occurrence rather than environment-richness associations — the article notes co-occurrence may reflect 'a common response to an external driver' http://edamontology.org/topic_3452 Statistical correlation of WGCNA subnetwork taxon richness/member profiles from an eDNA seawater time-series against measured Monterey Bay environmental variables (chlorophyll a, sea surface temperature) using Spearman rank correlation, to test whether seasonal subnetworks track environmental drivers. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-14105-1
skills.summary: Statistical correlation of WGCNA subnetwork taxon richness/member profiles from an eDNA seawater time-series against measured Monterey Bay environmental variables (chlorophyll a, sea surface temperature) using Spearman rank correlation, to test whether seasonal subnetworks track environmental drivers.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data or an unclustered feature table — the subnetwork membership must already exist from the upstream WGCNA community-network-analysis step Environmental variables and eDNA time points are not sample-aligned (no matched dates), since rank correlation requires paired observations The goal is inferring direct predator-prey interactions from co-occurrence rather than environment-richness associations — the article notes co-occurrence may reflect 'a common response to an external driver'

skills.description: Use when profiling bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, or viruses from metagenomic shotgun sequencing data, especially when accurate quantification of uncharacterized species (uSGBs/MAGs without cultured isolates) is required.
skills.name: marker-gene-based-abundance-estimation
skills.search_text: marker-gene-based-abundance-estimation Use when profiling bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, or viruses from metagenomic shotgun sequencing data, especially when accurate quantification of uncharacterized species (uSGBs/MAGs without cultured isolates) is required. Profiling under-characterized environmental or nonhost-associated microbial communities, which remain highly enriched for sequences not captured even by current uSGBs Extensive viral or eukaryotic microbial profiling, since current methods do not extensively incorporate viral or eukaryotic sequences due to their unique genomic architectures and quality control requirements Requiring reads to be assigned to a functional or full-genome reference rather than clade-specific markers (the profiler explains ~20% more reads in human gut but is marker-based, not whole-genome) http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Profile species-level relative abundances from shotgun metagenomes using clade-specific marker genes with MetaPhlAn 4, whose marker set covers 26,970 species-level genome bins (SGBs) including 4,992 taxonomically unidentified uSGBs from a curated collection of 1.01 M prokaryotic reference and metagenome-assembled genomes. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41587-023-01688-w
skills.summary: Profile species-level relative abundances from shotgun metagenomes using clade-specific marker genes with MetaPhlAn 4, whose marker set covers 26,970 species-level genome bins (SGBs) including 4,992 taxonomically unidentified uSGBs from a curated collection of 1.01 M prokaryotic reference and metagenome-assembled genomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Profiling under-characterized environmental or nonhost-associated microbial communities, which remain highly enriched for sequences not captured even by current uSGBs Extensive viral or eukaryotic microbial profiling, since current methods do not extensively incorporate viral or eukaryotic sequences due to their unique genomic architectures and quality control requirements Requiring reads to be assigned to a functional or full-genome reference rather than clade-specific markers (the profiler explains ~20% more reads in human gut but is marker-based, not whole-genome)

skills.description: Use when you need species-level relative-abundance profiles and explainable-read fractions from FASTQ shotgun metagenomes, especially to compare marker versions across environments (human gut, rumen, wild mice, ocean).
skills.name: marker-gene-based-species-quantification
skills.search_text: marker-gene-based-species-quantification Use when you need species-level relative-abundance profiles and explainable-read fractions from FASTQ shotgun metagenomes, especially to compare marker versions across environments (human gut, rumen, wild mice, ocean). The input is already a species-level abundance table and no re-profiling or version comparison is needed The goal is comprehensive read-level or functional (pathway/gene) profiling — marker-gene profiling quantifies clade abundance, not every sequence; use functional profilers like HUMAnN instead The community is dominated by viral or eukaryotic sequences, which the current SGB/marker set does not extensively incorporate http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Quantify species-level microbial relative abundance (bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, viruses) from shotgun metagenomes using clade-specific marker genes, as implemented in MetaPhlAn 4, whose extended SGB/marker set (26,970 SGBs incl. 4,992 unidentified uSGBs) also profiles uncharacterized taxa. metabarcoding/v1 10.1038/s41587-023-01688-w
skills.summary: Quantify species-level microbial relative abundance (bacteria, archaea, eukaryotes, viruses) from shotgun metagenomes using clade-specific marker genes, as implemented in MetaPhlAn 4, whose extended SGB/marker set (26,970 SGBs incl. 4,992 unidentified uSGBs) also profiles uncharacterized taxa.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a species-level abundance table and no re-profiling or version comparison is needed The goal is comprehensive read-level or functional (pathway/gene) profiling — marker-gene profiling quantifies clade abundance, not every sequence; use functional profilers like HUMAnN instead The community is dominated by viral or eukaryotic sequences, which the current SGB/marker set does not extensively incorporate

skills.description: Use when starting from raw paired-end NextSeq FASTQ files of 16S or COI amplicons and the goal is an error-filtered, merged, chimera-removed MOTU count table per marker gene.
skills.name: marker-gene-metabarcoding-processing
skills.search_text: marker-gene-metabarcoding-processing Use when starting from raw paired-end NextSeq FASTQ files of 16S or COI amplicons and the goal is an error-filtered, merged, chimera-removed MOTU count table per marker gene.
